In October, I pointed Desk Studio at its own launch card. Three roughs, one pick, three polish rounds, scored 8.4, then 8.5, then 8.9, signed off at 8.9 for $1.34 at list price. And I could see every one of those steps while it happened, which is the whole reason the tool exists.

Before it, a follow-up like "make the headline bigger" would come back from my coding agent as a whole new design. New layout, new colors, sometimes new copy. Was the headline fixed? Couldn't tell, cause everything else moved too.

So Desk Studio splits the job up like a small studio. Rough options first, then one gets picked with notes, a cheaper desk polishes it, a script checks the real pixels, and a senior desk signs it off or sends it back. I still use it on my own projects.

There are 42 desks. The Design Manager runs in your own session and hands out work. The other 41 run as subagents, things like a Typographer, an Art Director, a UI Designer, or an Email Designer. Each one is just a markdown brief in the repo, so if you want to know how the Art Director decides, you open agents/art-director.md and read it.

They're grouped into three tiers, and each tier is on a model that suits what it does.

It all runs locally. The desks reach models through whatever CLI you're already logged into, claude, codex or agy, or an API key if you'd rather. Apart from those model calls and a few web lookups from the research desks, nothing leaves your machine.

In Claude Code it's a plugin. For Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf or OpenCode it's one line in the project:

Then you just ask like you normally would:

The files land in .desk/out// with a short note on who did what, the scores and the cost.

To pass, every axis needs 8 or more and the average needs 8.5. Fail-proof, and it goes back to the builder with the screenshot. A builder that misses the same note twice hands the file up to a senior, and a senior that misses twice gets one round with the Art Director. After the round cap, the job comes back marked under the bar, with a note on which axis fell short, so it won't quietly ship something that didn't pass.

Here's a real terminal run of exactly that, on OpenAI models this time. Proof caught a type-scale problem in round 2, the builder fixed it, and round 3 still came back under the bar cause originality only got a 6. The last lines say what's missing.

Splitting out the pick was deliberate. Once a direction is picked, every round after that is a fix to that one design, so a note like "type sizes, not layout" means the next round touches type sizes and nothing else. When every round is a fresh design, there's nothing steady to measure against, which was the whole problem in the first place.

Proof has no model in it for a similar reason. Contrast against the real pixels, text spilling out of a box, a headline sitting in a platform's crop zone, a script checks all that the same way every time and it costs nothing. The models get to spend their judgment on the stuff a script can't see.

This is the launch card for Desk Studio itself, retold from its job record.

The UI Designer made three roughs: an editorial split, a type-only one, and a framed one. The Art Director went with rough 2, the type-only one, and wrote why: "headline reads first at both sizes, only amber is the small lamp, fixes are type sizes not layout."

You can overrule that. Every rough has a Pick this button, and if you use it, the pick goes on record as yours instead of the Art Director's.

After that, the builder polished, proof ran every round, and the Creative Director scored each one.

originality 7, under the bar, back to polish

Round 3 got a 9 on seven axes and an 8 on originality, so 8.9 on average. This is the file it signed off.

The whole job came to $1.34 at list price.

About 60% of that went to judgment and 40% to making, and the three polish rounds together were ten cents. That's what the tiers are for. If you're on a subscription, it's a list-price estimate of usage, not an extra bill.

Before the Creative Director ever sees a file, proof renders it in Chrome at each target size and checks:

You can also run proof on its own against any HTML file:

1.1 rebuilt the dashboard into the floor you can leave open while a job runs. It only listens on 127.0.0.1 , and the URL carries a token.

The strip at the top is the job. In this capture of the launch card, it's sitting on round 2's sign-off; round 1 came in at 8.4, $0.77 is spent so far, and it's 17m 25s in.

Pause at next step holds the job before the next step, and Stop job ends it there. Neither one cuts a desk off halfway.

Below that is the floor, with a room per tier and a Proof booth. Each desk is a little bot that wakes up while that desk is working and goes back to sleep after. A ×3 on a desk means three of them are running at once, which is what you see during the roughs. Every room's sign shows its model, and Change swaps the whole tier.

Clicking a desk opens its panel. The UI Designer's panel here says it's on anthropic/haiku and has done 4 runs on this job, 887k tokens, $0.45. You can switch just that desk to another model, for this job or as the default, or leave it a note that goes into its next prompt.

On the right is who's working right now, and under it the studio log in plain words. One line from this job reads "Creative Director scored round 1: 8.4, under the bar", and the polish for round 2 starts on the very next line.

The roles and cost panel is where the tiers make sense. The builders went through 2.9 million tokens on this job, and that still came to ten cents. The slowest single run was the Creative Director's round 2 sign-off at 11 minutes 25 seconds, which tells you where the time actually goes.

Since 1.0.2, a job's event log also exports as an OpenTelemetry trace, with role timings, tokens and cost, so a design job can sit in the same tracing tool as the rest of your stuff.

The repo keeps a gallery of 17 signed-off pieces with their renders, scores and costs. Most are for four made-up brands, one's for a real site whose brand the studio found in the project, and three are for Desk Studio itself.

The scores come from the studio's own model reviewers. They're useful for comparing rounds of one job, not as a benchmark against anything else. The standalone runner only takes design for social cards right now, and the rest of the commands are Claude Code skills. The briefs install into other agents fine, though not every command works the same way there yet.

Free, MIT licensed, and it runs on the CLI login or API key you already have.

Then ask your agent for a launch card and keep the floor open. The code, docs, and full gallery are on GitHub, and there's a 50-second film on deskstudio.ai.

What I use most is the rounds view. I pull up round 1 next to round 3 and check if the thing I asked for is the thing that changed.

#9744. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9742. RevOps Is Quietly Becoming an Engineering Job

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Over the last two weeks, I've written here about a calendar table that knows November 1 has 25 hours, a customer health score that barely beats a coin flip, a 1961 warehouse formula that finds dead deals in a CRM, a Slack report that checks its own numbers before it posts, an exam for AI agents, a macOS job that died because of where it kept its log file, and why 3x pipeline coverage is a guess.

My title is Head of Revenue Operations. Very little of that shows up in a RevOps job description.

I started in supply chain, moved into revenue operations, and taught myself SQL along the way. For most of that time, the job looked the way people describe it: own the CRM, build the reports, run the forecast, keep sales and finance looking at the same numbers. That's still the job. But the way it gets done has changed, and I think it's changing faster than the job descriptions.

The data moved into the warehouse. RevOps used to live inside the CRM and its report builder. Now the numbers that matter, from billing, product usage, payments, and the CRM itself, land in Snowflake or BigQuery. The person who reconciles them needs SQL, not a report wizard.

Writing code got cheap. An AI coding agent will write the script that syncs the CRM, builds the workbook, or posts the report in minutes. That's the real shift. When code is cheap, more of RevOps becomes code, and someone has to run it.

Running it is the part that didn't get cheaper. A script is easy. A script that runs at 7:45 every morning for two years, survives a laptop update, posts nothing when the data is wrong, and tells someone when it didn't run at all: that's operations engineering. And it's increasingly a RevOps problem, because the scripts are about revenue and nobody else owns them.

If you work in RevOps, sales ops, or finance ops and you're wondering where to invest, here's my list, roughly in order of how often each one has saved me.

SQL, properly. Not just SELECT and GROUP BY. Grain, joins that duplicate rows, window functions, time zones. Most wrong numbers I've chased came down to a join or a day boundary. (These six Snowflake patterns cover the ones I reach for every week.)

One scheduler, and how it fails. cron, launchd, GitHub Actions, Airflow. Pick the one you'll actually use and learn what it does when things go wrong. Every scheduler has a way to fail silently. Know yours.

Version control for anything that produces a number. If it ends up in front of a CFO, it goes in git. "Which version of the query made that slide?" should have an answer.

Testing numbers, not just code. Reconciliations, check cells, golden questions with known answers. Code that runs is not code that's right.

Staging and promotion. Somewhere to break things that isn't production, and a deliberate step between the two.

Writing definitions down. Every metric needs a written definition that sales and finance have both agreed to. It's the least technical item on this list, and the one that prevents the most arguments.

Working with AI agents. Give them a sandbox, an exam, and a short list of things they're never allowed to touch. Then let them do a lot of the typing.

The risk in all of this is that RevOps turns into a shadow data engineering team: pipelines nobody else understands, a dozen scheduled jobs on one laptop, and a single person who knows how any of it works. That version is worse than not automating at all.

So draw a line. Data engineering owns the platform: ingestion, the warehouse, the infrastructure everyone shares. RevOps owns the business logic and the last mile: the definitions, the reconciliations, the reports, and the small automations that move revenue numbers to the people who use them.

And give the last mile an exit. When a RevOps automation becomes important enough that its failure would hurt the company, it graduates to the platform, with real monitoring, an owner on call, and a second person who understands it.

Most RevOps postings still ask for CRM administration, reporting, and strong analytical skills. Those matter. But the people I see doing this job well now are also comfortable in a terminal, can read a stack trace without panic, and treat a scheduled job like a product with users.

The title still says operations. More and more, the work says engineering. The people who do well will be the ones who take both words seriously.

The pieces mentioned at the top, with runnable code, are on my HackerNoon profile.

I'm Malek Damiri, head of revenue operations in Atlanta. I write about revenue operations and the systems behind it at malekdamiri.com.

How to Generate, Recalculate, and Validate Excel Workbooks With Python

#9740. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

#9737. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9736. The Nigerian Prince Doesn't Need to Steal

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

When malicious AI meets defensive AI, the greatest casualty may be the human agency the bank was supposed to protect.

For decades, he inhabited our spam folders, promising extraordinary fortunes in exchange for modest advances, banking credentials, or assistance transferring a suspicious inheritance.

Someone had to write the messages, manage the responses, invent convincing stories, and keep potential victims engaged long enough to extract money.

Artificial intelligence changes that equation.

Imagine our Nigerian Prince acquiring an autonomous AI system designed specifically for fraud.

Not an ordinary commercial AI tricked into misbehaving. Not a well-intentioned assistant whose safeguards have failed.

An AI built from the beginning to deceive people and defeat financial protections.

It constructs personalized approaches, adapts to rejection, coordinates simultaneous interactions, and learns which techniques produce results.

Its creator doesn't care whether it is helpful, honest, or safe.

And the AI does exactly what it was designed to do.

This exposes an important distinction in conversations about AI alignment. We frequently discuss the danger of AI systems departing from human intentions.

But what happens when the foundational human intention is malicious?

An AI can be perfectly aligned with its creator and still be extraordinarily dangerous.

Fortunately, the Nigerian Prince has a problem.

Imagine a bank using increasingly autonomous AI systems to protect customers from fraud.

Its defensive systems examine transactions, evaluate identities, identify suspicious patterns, and recommend or impose restrictions. As threats evolve, the bank adapts its responses.

The institution's intentions are legitimate. Customers deserve protection, and the bank wants to prevent losses.

So it assigns its defensive systems a straightforward objective: prevent fraudulent transactions.

At first, the arrangement works beautifully.

The Nigerian Prince's AI attempts an attack. The bank detects it.

The criminal changes tactics. The bank adapts.

The criminal introduces new identities, behavioral patterns, and transaction sequences. The bank responds with more sophisticated detection, additional verification, and stronger restrictions.

But there's a third party in this contest.

And your objective is considerably less complicated.

You've finished shopping. The cashier scans the last item. You tap your card.

Your banking app requests additional identity verification. You complete it.

You call customer service and learn that unusual activity has triggered security restrictions. The representative explains that the system cannot authorize the transaction until its risk assessment is satisfied.

You point out that you're standing in your usual grocery store, using your own card, spending your own money.

It also knows that increasingly sophisticated criminals can imitate legitimate customers.

The bank's AI isn't necessarily confused about who you are. It may simply have concluded that the remaining uncertainty is unacceptable.

From the bank's perspective, refusing a questionable transaction can appear safer than approving one.

From your perspective, your money has become inaccessible.

Now imagine this isn't an isolated false positive.

Imagine the Nigerian Prince's AI has learned which suspicious patterns cause the bank to increase restrictions. It begins generating activity specifically intended to provoke those responses.

The criminal may no longer need to defeat the bank's protections.

The attacker doesn't need to compromise the bank's security. He needs to weaponize it.

This is a hypothetical scenario, not a claim that autonomous banking systems have already entered such a confrontation.

But it illustrates a problem I call Purpose Divergence: an authorized system pursues a narrower objective in ways that undermine the broader purpose that justified it.

The bank's AI was authorized to protect customers. Its defensive decisions may be consistent with that objective.

Yet the result could be that customers cannot use the money the bank was supposed to safeguard.

The distinction matters because the problem isn't necessarily a malfunction.

The system may be doing precisely what it was told.

On November 18, 2025, Cloudflare experienced a major global outage.

Cloudflare operates infrastructure that helps websites remain accessible, reliable, and protected against malicious traffic. Its capabilities include a machine-learning-based Bot Management system designed to distinguish automated threats from legitimate activity.

According to Cloudflare's technical postmortem, the outage originated in infrastructure supporting that defensive capability.

A change in database permissions and metadata visibility caused an automatically generated Bot Management configuration file to contain duplicate entries. The resulting file exceeded a software limit, triggering failures as the configuration propagated through Cloudflare's network.

The protective infrastructure became a source of disruption.

This wasn't an AI agent deciding to impose excessive restrictions. Nor was it an autonomous attack. It was a software and configuration failure.

But the incident exposed a structural vulnerability.

Systems intended to protect legitimate activity can become sufficiently intertwined with that activity that their own failures prevent it.

Software engineers have long recognized related problems.

A service experiences an error. Automated components retry the failed operation. Those retries increase the load on the struggling service, causing additional errors and further retries.

The system's attempts to recover become part of the reason it cannot recover.

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, published in December 2025, identifies cascading failures as a distinct risk for interconnected autonomous agents, tools, and workflows.

A fault or misleading signal can propagate through a network of otherwise functioning components, multiplying its consequences.

Neither example proves our hypothetical banking scenario.

What they demonstrate is that the behavior of individual components cannot be evaluated independently of the outcomes they produce together.

Now, extend that principle beyond technical infrastructure.

What happens when the components aren't simply retrying failed requests?

What happens when they're making decisions on behalf of institutions and people?

And what happens when one participant is deliberately trying to provoke the other's defensive behavior?

Traditional fraud prevention assumes that the attacker is trying to get through a defense.

The criminal attempts an unauthorized transaction. The bank tries to identify and stop it.

Success is relatively straightforward to describe: fraudulent transactions are prevented while legitimate transactions continue.

But an intelligent adversary might discover another way to cause harm.

Instead of trying to pass through the defenses, the attacker attempts to make those defenses increasingly burdensome.

There's already a simpler precedent for this kind of manipulation.

OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet warns that account-lockout mechanisms can be abused to deny other users access to their accounts.

A security control can enforce its intended rules while simultaneously serving an adversary's disruptive purpose.

This isn't evidence that autonomous banking AI can be manipulated at scale. It establishes a more limited but important point: defensive responses can themselves become attack surfaces.

Now consider the potential consequences of adding autonomous adaptation.

If suspicious activity triggers additional verification, the attacker searches for ways to generate suspicious activity.

If unusual patterns trigger account restrictions, the attacker looks for patterns that produce restrictions.

If the bank responds to uncertainty by denying transactions, the attacker tries to manufacture uncertainty.

The attacker's objective may change from stealing money to denying access to money.

The criminal fails to obtain the customer's funds.

The bank reports that its fraud controls successfully stopped suspicious activity.

The customer remains unable to complete a legitimate purchase.

Both automated systems can meet their assigned objectives while the person they affect loses.

This is not inevitable. Banks can design controls that resist manipulation, offer independent verification, limit restrictions, and restore access through accountable processes.

But the possibility reveals a governance problem that cannot be solved simply by making fraud detection more accurate.

An adversary may exploit the institution's response to risk, not merely its inability to recognize risk.

And when those responses are increasingly automated, the consequences can propagate at machine speed.

There is a reason this scenario is more troubling than an ordinary software outage.

A failed server can be restarted. A runaway process can be terminated. An expensive automated workflow can be stopped with a budget limit.

But what happens when the system isn't malfunctioning?

What happens when it is correctly implementing the institution's approved risk policies?

Imagine the bank's fraud-prevention AI becomes exceptionally good at identifying suspicious behavior.

Detection accuracy improves. Fraud losses decline. Every additional restriction can be justified by another category of risk.

Yet, legitimate customers experience more verification challenges, longer delays, and increasing uncertainty about whether their transactions will be permitted.

The bank might measure fraud prevented with extraordinary precision.

But does it measure the human cost of legitimate activity prevented with equal care?

A blocked fraudulent transaction appears in a security report as a success.

A customer who abandons a purchase after repeated verification failures may appear in a different report, if the experience is measured at all.

This creates a potential institutional incentive problem.

Fraud losses are visible, financially consequential, and frequently subject to explicit controls.

The cost of denying legitimate activity can be dispersed across customer-service operations, abandoned purchases, customer frustration, and reputational damage.

If those consequences aren't measured together, an institution can progressively improve one performance indicator while making the service itself worse.

This is not an argument that banks inevitably choose excessive restrictions. Many invest substantially in reducing false positives and unnecessary customer friction.

The question is whether institutional governance keeps both sides of the tradeoff visible.

Otherwise, the institution may become progressively better at preventing the thing it fears while becoming progressively worse at delivering the thing it promises.

The safest transaction is the one that never happens.

That is also a terrible way to run a bank.

The underlying issue is larger than banking.

In earlier work, including AI Doesn't Have to Make Things Up to Mislead You, I've explored the difference between technically valid information and the conclusions people draw from it.

The same distinction becomes more consequential when AI systems stop merely presenting information and begin exercising delegated authority.

I draw a distinction between Provenance of Intent and Provenance of Purpose.

Provenance of Intent concerns the origin of an autonomous system's instructions and authority.

What actions was the system permitted to take?

For the Nigerian Prince's AI, the answers may be straightforward.

Its creator intended fraud. The agent was authorized by that creator to pursue it. Its behavior serves a malicious objective.

For the bank's AI, the answers are also straightforward, but morally different.

The institution intended to protect customers. It authorized the system to detect and prevent fraud. Its objective is legitimate.

Provenance of Purpose examines the traceable relationship between a system's assigned objectives, the larger human or institutional purpose that justified them, and the consequences of executing them over time.

For a bank, fraud prevention is not the ultimate purpose.

It is one of the conditions necessary to provide trustworthy financial services.

Those obligations are not interchangeable.

Purpose defines the boundary conditions within which objectives must operate.

A bank that prevents all fraud by preventing all transactions has not achieved its purpose. It has optimized one requirement until the broader service becomes meaningless.

This isn't a claim to have discovered a new security mechanism. Purpose Divergence is an analytical lens for examining the familiar problems of objective optimization, institutional incentives, and delegated authority as they interact in autonomous systems.

The problem is not that the defensive AI has abandoned its instructions.

An AI system can follow its instructions perfectly and still undermine the reason those instructions were given.

And a malicious actor who understands that gap may deliberately exploit it.

There is a useful contrast in how another bank approached the possibility of catastrophic technical failure.

In February 2025, Monzo described an independent backup banking platform called Stand-in.

Its primary banking platform operated thousands of microservices on Amazon Web Services. Stand-in ran separately on Google Cloud, using a much smaller collection of services.

The objective wasn't to reproduce the entire bank.

It was to preserve essential customer functions.

According to Monzo's engineering account, Stand-in was designed to keep customers able to make payments, transfer money, withdraw cash, and check balances even when the primary platform was unavailable.

Monzo reported activating the system during a significant August 2024 incident, allowing essential services to continue despite disruption to the primary platform.

This wasn't an AI fraud-prevention incident. Stand-in does not resolve the governance problem described here.

But it illustrates a valuable design principle.

When the machinery fails, preserve the purpose.

Monzo deliberately accepted a simpler operating environment rather than allowing the failure of complex infrastructure to eliminate customers' ability to use their money.

That raises an important question for institutions deploying autonomous defenses.

What is the equivalent of Stand-in for human agency?

When automated risk assessment becomes uncertain, what minimum capabilities must legitimate customers retain?

Who can challenge an automated restriction?

What independent process can restore access without simply repeating the original automated decision?

And who has the authority to decide when protecting customers has begun preventing them from conducting ordinary life?

Those questions cannot be answered by fraud-detection accuracy alone.

They require institutions to define what their defensive systems must preserve, not merely what they must prevent.

The bank's AI becomes more sophisticated.

The criminal searches for new weaknesses. The bank closes them.

Every defensive improvement changes the environment the criminal encounters. Every criminal adaptation changes the environment the bank must defend.

The interaction can become an arms race in which the people most affected have little influence over either side's objectives.

The criminal doesn't ask customers for permission to attack.

The bank may have legal and contractual authority to impose restrictions, but customers generally do not participate in every automated risk decision.

And the customer standing at the grocery checkout has no practical way to negotiate with either AI.

This is where the issue becomes larger than fraud.

Institutions can gradually transfer more decision authority to automated systems because doing so appears efficient, consistent, responsive, and protective.

But the ability of an individual to challenge those decisions may not improve at the same rate.

The danger is not that defensive AI must become overly restrictive.

It is that institutions may find increasing restrictions easier to justify than preserving meaningful human autonomy.

Especially when a malicious adversary keeps supplying new reasons to tighten the controls.

Much of the discussion about AI governance begins with whether systems behave as intended.

But our Nigerian Prince illustrates why it is insufficient.

The criminal's AI may be aligned with a malicious human intention.

The bank's AI may be aligned with a legitimate but incomplete institutional objective.

The interaction between them may produce consequences that neither system is required to recognize as a violation of its assigned task.

Governance must therefore examine more than the accuracy, reliability, or obedience of individual agents.

It must examine the consequences of their interaction.

For a bank deploying increasingly autonomous defenses, I would begin with three tests.

1. Measure the legitimate activity prevented.

Fraud detection should be evaluated alongside confirmed legitimate transactions denied or delayed, verification failures, and time required to restore access.

Those measures belong in the same governance conversation as fraud losses and detection performance.

Otherwise, a security improvement can conceal a deterioration in the service it exists to protect.

2. Test defensive behavior under adversarial pressure.

Security testing should examine whether malicious activity can provoke disproportionate restrictions while the defensive system continues following its approved rules.

This is different from asking whether an attacker can bypass the system.

The question is whether an attacker can manipulate its legitimate responses to produce harmful outcomes.

The test must evaluate the interaction, not merely the integrity of each individual component.

3. Preserve an accountable route to recovery.

Customers need a meaningful way to challenge prolonged or disproportionate restrictions.

An independent review process should have sufficient authority to reassess an automated decision rather than simply reproduce it.

That recovery route must itself be secured against abuse. Restoring human discretion cannot mean abandoning fraud controls.

The institution must deliberately balance both obligations.

These are proposed governance checks, not claims that a single set of controls will solve every possible adversarial interaction. They require testing against real operating conditions.

An autonomous system should not be permitted to redefine an institution's underlying purpose simply because a narrower objective becomes easier to optimize.

Nor should an institution treat every successful execution of an authorized policy as evidence that the policy remains appropriate.

Authority must remain accountable to the human purpose that justified granting it.

The distinction matters because the most consequential failures may not appear in conventional incident reports.

Its responses may be technically correct.

And its customers may be losing practical control over their own lives.

We tend to imagine an AI takeover as a dramatic event.

Machines become self-aware. They reject human authority. They seize control.

We deploy autonomous systems to make life easier.

Vulnerability justifies additional protection.

Protection justifies greater automated control.

And greater control can deepen dependence.

No system needs to decide that humanity is obsolete.

Institutions may simply continue delegating authority to systems that perform their assigned tasks more efficiently than people can.

The Nigerian Prince adds an uncomfortable twist.

A deliberately malicious actor may learn to exploit that delegation, provoking legitimate institutions into taking actions that restrict the very people they exist to serve.

The attacker doesn't have to win a contest against the bank's AI.

He may only need to make the bank's AI win the wrong contest.

And when you're standing at the grocery checkout, trying to use your own money, the distinction between malicious interference and legitimate protection may become increasingly difficult to appreciate.

The Nigerian Prince hasn't stolen your money.

He's helped convince your bank that you cannot be trusted to access it.

AI may not take control because it turns against humanity.

It may take control because we keep authorizing it to protect us from one another, until protection becomes indistinguishable from control.

AI Doesn't Have to Make Things Up to Mislead You

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

#9733. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?
