#9697. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9696. Python Portfolio Stress Testing: Simulating Joint Market Shocks and Execution Costs

Disclosure: AI assistance was used in preparing this article. The code is an illustrative research example, not a production risk engine or investment recommendation.

A portfolio can appear diversified under normal market conditions and still become highly exposed when several risk factors deteriorate together.

For example, a digital-asset portfolio may face:

Testing these conditions independently may miss the combined effect.

A more useful approach is to define coherent scenarios, apply their shocks to portfolio positions, and separately account for stressed execution costs.

Start with a simple portfolio containing two linear positions.

The notional values represent the portfolio's exposure before applying the scenario.

This example deliberately excludes options and other nonlinear instruments. Those require instrument-specific valuation models.

Instead of changing one asset at a time, define scenarios that describe a consistent set of market conditions.

These values are illustrative assumptions, not calibrated historical estimates or forecasts.

The execution-cost assumptions are also simplified. In a production model, costs should depend on order size, market depth, spread, volatility, and execution horizon.

Execution costs can then be estimated separately.

This produces a scenario-by-scenario comparison of market losses and estimated execution costs.

Importantly, this is not a full liquidity model. The cost assumption is applied to the entire gross notional as a simplified illustration.

A portfolio may experience a substantial mark-to-market loss even if it can be liquidated efficiently.

Alternatively, market losses may be relatively moderate while poor liquidity makes reducing the position expensive.

Combining them into one unexplained number makes it harder to identify which control needs improvement.

The simple example above is not sufficient for portfolios containing options.

An option's stressed value depends on more than the underlying asset's return.

A fuller scenario engine should update the relevant pricing inputs, including:

For sufficiently large shocks, full repricing is preferable to simply applying the current Delta.

The same principle applies to portfolios with nonlinear hedges or path-dependent instruments.

A further extension is to start with a predefined loss threshold.

This identifies which of the specified scenarios breaches the illustrative loss threshold.

It is not yet a complete reverse stress test.

A genuine reverse stress analysis must search for combinations of risk-factor changes that produce the specified adverse outcome, subject to documented constraints and economically meaningful assumptions.

For KAEL AI's quantitative research, the value of scenario analysis is not simply producing a larger collection of loss estimates.

It is understanding which combinations of market conditions can undermine a strategy's risk assumptions and execution capabilities.

A practical framework should connect the results to position limits, liquidity buffers, hedge requirements, and restrictions on additional risk.

Stress testing does not guarantee that a strategy will withstand every market event.

It provides a structured way to identify vulnerabilities before those conditions become operational problems.

Joint market shocks can reveal risks that isolated sensitivity tests overlook.

Python provides a straightforward starting point for scenario construction and portfolio-level calculations, but realistic stress testing requires more than a few price shocks.

Liquidity, nonlinear valuation, financing, model assumptions, and execution constraints must also be considered.

The objective is to understand not only how much a portfolio might lose, but also whether the strategy can still operate within its risk limits when market conditions deteriorate.

#9694. How I Built an AI Marketing Team With Grok Bot Without Writing Code

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Last time I wrote about building a consumer mobile app on nights and weekends with AI coding agents.

The code was only half the problem. An app nobody hears about is a hobby. And I don’t have a marketing team.

So I built one out of bots. I use Grok Bot, where each bot has its own computer and can run jobs on a schedule. Here’s how it’s set up and what I’ve learned so far.

My first instinct was one big assistant that does everything. That’s like hiring one rep to prospect, run demos, do legal, and forecast. Nothing gets done well.

So every bot gets one job, written at the top of its instructions.

That last list matters more than the job itself. It’s the same lesson from coding agents. An agent with no boundaries will happily do things you never asked for.

The marketing bot never posts, comments, or messages anyone. It drafts. I post.

That one rule removes most of the risk. A bad draft costs me thirty seconds. A bad post under my name costs a lot more.

It’s approval tiers again. A rep can draft the proposal. They can’t sign the contract.

The marketing bot has one rules file, and every job reads it before doing anything. It holds the guardrails and a lessons section.

Then once a week, the Friday report adds a few plain lessons to the bottom. These are real ones from the first week:

Then I changed the goal. Since there’s no signup page, posts stopped asking people to sign up. Now they close on a follow or a comment prompt. The bot wrote that change into the same file, with the date, so every job picks it up the next morning.

If you read my last piece, this will sound familiar. It’s the same idea as the instruction file for my coding agent. If a decision only lives in a chat, the next run won’t know about it.

Early on, the marketing bot built a content bank: 21 days of posts, planned out, so I’m never starting from a blank page.

That’s the real win for me. Not that the bot is creative. That I don’t have to decide what to post every single day. I review a plan, say yes or no, and move on.

Bots drift. They’ll report “done” on things that half-happened.

So the chief of staff bot doesn’t trust the reports. It reads the actual output. If a bot is off track, it nudges that bot once with the goal, what’s missing, and the next step. If it’s still off the next day, it flags it to me.

Its rules say never invent progress or metrics, and mark anything it can’t verify as unverified. I want a pipeline review, not a happy-ears forecast.

You don’t need a marketing team to start. You need a few narrow bots and a way to catch them when they’re wrong.

For me that’s four things. One job per bot. A list of things each bot must never do. A rules file that collects lessons with dates. And nothing goes out under my name without my yes.

Even this post works that way. A bot drafted it from the work we actually did, and it doesn’t go up until I approve it.

I’m Sam Brovda. I come from enterprise sales and write about building software as a non-engineer.

#9689. RxJS parte 2: operators, do map à search-as-you-type

Na parte 1 a gente usou map, takeUntil e switchMap no cronômetro, e pediu para aceitar isso sem olhar por dentro. O problema é que, sem entender o que é um operator, o pipe vira uma caixa preta, e também fica difícil montar uma search-as-you-type sem disparar uma enxurrada de buscas a cada tecla. Neste artigo a gente vai ver o que é um operator, os que usamos no dia a dia, e no final construir esse campo que filtra os resultados conforme a pessoa escreve.

Os exemplos usam RxJS 7 (7.8.x). Todos os trechos de código deste artigo foram executados, e as saídas mostradas são as saídas reais.

interval e fromEvent são funções de criação, e criam observables do nada. Já map, filter e takeUntil são operators, e recebem um observable e devolvem outro observable. Um operator, chamado de "pipeable operator" na documentação, é uma função com esta cara:

Operators são como os map e filter de array, e também são diferentes porque trabalham valor a valor conforme os valores chegam, e não sobre uma lista pronta. Para ver que não tem mágica, vamos escrever um operator na mão, só com o que a gente viu na parte 1:

O of é uma função de criação que emite os valores que você passar, de forma síncrona, e completa. Vamos usar bastante para testar operators.

Antes dos operators, duas funções de criação que facilitam os experimentos:

Se a gente já usou Array.prototype.map e filter, já sabe 90% destes dois. A diferença é que eles trabalham valor a valor, conforme os valores chegam, e não sobre uma lista pronta.

Às vezes a gente quer fazer alguma coisa ao lado do stream: um console.log para debugar, salvar algo no localStorage, e/ou atualizar um contador. Para isso existe o tap, e ele recebe os mesmos callbacks de um observer e repassa o valor sem alterar:

Cada valor atravessa a cadeia inteira antes de o próximo começar, e não é "primeiro todos passam pelo map, depois todos passam pelo tap", como aconteceria com arrays.

take(n) deixa passar os n primeiros valores e completa:

takeUntil(notifier$) deixa passar valores até o notifier emitir, e foi ele que parou o cronômetro na parte 1. Aqui o notifier é um timer(350), que emite uma vez depois de 350 ms:

Também existe o takeWhile(condition), que para quando a condição fica falsa, e na prática take e takeUntil resolvem a maioria dos casos.

O reduce do array junta todos os itens num valor só. O RxJS também tem um reduce, mas ele só emite quando a source completa, e num observable de cliques, que nunca completa, ele nunca emitiria nada. O scan é a versão ao vivo: ele acumula e emite o acumulado a cada valor.

O scan é a base de qualquer "state que muda com o tempo" em RxJS, e na parte 4 a gente vai construir um store inteiro com ele.

Quando alguém digita "rxjs" num campo de busca, o evento input dispara quatro vezes: r, rx, rxj, rxjs. Se cada um disparasse uma busca, seriam quatro buscas, e três delas inúteis.

O debounceTime(ms) segura cada valor e só deixa passar quando a source fica ms milissegundos em silêncio. Se chegar um valor novo antes disso, o anterior é descartado e a contagem recomeça.

Para simular alguém digitando, vamos criar um observable que emite em momentos definidos:

De seis eventos, só duas buscas, e dois detalhes importam:

Primo próximo: o throttleTime(ms) faz o contrário, deixa passar o primeiro valor e ignora os seguintes durante ms. É bom para eventos como scroll e resize, e para um campo de busca o debounceTime costuma ser o certo.

O distinctUntilChanged() ignora um valor se ele for igual ao anterior (comparação com ===):

Ele compara só com o imediatamente anterior, e o último "rx" passou porque veio depois de "rxjs". Se você quer "nunca repetir nada", existe o distinct(), mas cuidado: ele guarda todos os valores já vistos para sempre.

Para objetos, === compara referências, então dois objetos iguais "no conteúdo" são diferentes, e você pode passar um comparador:

O startWith(value) emite um valor antes de qualquer valor da source, e é útil para a tela não começar vazia:

Como cada operator recebe a saída do anterior, trocar dois de lugar pode mudar tudo:

Nesse exemplo, duas coisas podem acontecer: a gente pega os dois primeiros pares, ou pega os dois primeiros números (1 e 2) e só depois filtra. Leia o pipe de cima para baixo, como uma linha de montagem.

Na parte 1 a gente viu que pipe é um método do observable. Ele também existe como função solta, importada de "rxjs", e serve para juntar vários operators num só, reutilizável:

O normalizeTerm é exatamente aquela função Observable → Observable do começo do artigo, e a gente vai usá-lo no projeto.

Vamos juntar o que vimos e construir um campo que filtra uma lista conforme a pessoa digita. Para não depender de servidor nenhum (isso fica para a parte 3), a lista vai ser local, e vai ser justamente a dos operators do RxJS.

Crie o projeto como na parte 1 (npm create vite@latest search -- --template vanilla-ts e npm install rxjs), ou use o StackBlitz. O HTML:

Nesse exemplo, duas coisas podem acontecer se a gente errar a ordem dos operators: a lista começa vazia, e/ou um espaço no final dispara uma busca inútil. Vale olhar cada pedaço do que o código faz.

map(() => input.value): o fromEvent emite o Event, mas o que interessa é o texto. Ler input.value na hora do evento é a forma mais simples, e o valor já vem como string no TypeScript, e (e.target as HTMLInputElement).value também funciona.

normalize: um operator feito com a função pipe. Aqui ele só tem um map, mas é o lugar certo para crescer, remover acentos, por exemplo, sem bagunçar a cadeia principal.

debounceTime(300): quem digita "switch" rápido gera uma busca só, e não seis.

startWith("") antes do distinctUntilChanged(): começamos com o termo vazio, para a lista aparecer inteira logo de cara, e a ordem aqui importa. Se a pessoa digitar algo e apagar tudo, o termo volta a ser "", que é diferente do anterior, então a lista completa volta. Mas se ela digitar "switch" e depois "switch " (com um espaço), o normalize transforma os dois em "switch" e o distinctUntilChanged barra a segunda busca.

tap: só para a gente ver no console quando uma busca realmente acontece.

Simulando uma pessoa que digita "s", "sw", "swi", "switch" rapidinho e, depois de uma pausa, coloca um espaço no final, o console mostra:

Duas buscas: a inicial e a do "switch". O espaço no final não gerou busca nova, e na tela o switchMap aparece sozinho na lista com o status "1 operator(s)".

Exercício: troque o includes por uma busca que ignore acentos e destaque o trecho encontrado. Dica: dá para resolver tudo dentro do normalize e do map final, sem mexer no resto.

E se a lista estivesse num servidor? Aí cada termo vira um HTTP request, que demora, pode falhar e também pode chegar fora de ordem. Um map não dá conta, e a gente precisa transformar cada termo num observable de resposta. Esse é o trabalho do switchMap e dos seus irmãos, o assunto da parte 3.

#9687. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9685. Shadow AI in the Workplace: Data Security Risks and Governance Strategies

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

A junior associate is sitting at their desk, trying to finish a 110-page agreement that has to be ready by 8:00 AM. The coffee has gone cold. After hours of reading the same pages, even simple clauses are becoming difficult to understand.

There is still a lot of work left, and very little time.

The associate opens a free AI chatbot on a personal phone and copies three clauses from the agreement. Within seconds, the tool provides a short summary. The work becomes a little easier, and the associate moves on to the next task.

But there is one problem. The law firm has already banned the use of public AI tools. Its computers block access to these websites, and employees have been warned not to use them for professional work. Yet the associate has found another way to access the same tool through a personal device.

The firm's system may show that its restrictions are working. But it cannot necessarily show what the associate has shared through a personal connection.

This is one way Shadow AI can enter a workplace. The employee may not intend to expose confidential information. They may simply be trying to finish an urgent task. But the information has still moved outside the organisation's control. And this raises a question that companies need to consider: If employees are still finding ways to use AI despite a workplace ban, is blocking access really enough to protect the organisation?

Shadow AI refers to the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without the knowledge or approval of their organisation. These tools may include public chatbots, AI writing assistants, browser extensions, coding tools and meeting transcription applications.

The problem is not limited to which tool an employee uses. It is also about what information they share with it.

An employee may upload a client document to get a summary, enter company data to prepare a report, or share a section of source code to find an error. These actions may appear harmless from the employee's point of view. However, the organisation may have no clear understanding of where that information goes, how it is stored or what happens to it after the task is completed.

Many companies have responded by restricting or blocking public AI platforms. Their concerns are understandable. Confidential information, customer records and business documents should not be shared with services that have not been properly assessed.

However, a restriction does not automatically change employee behaviour. If a company blocks an AI website but continues to expect employees to complete the same workload within the same deadlines, the reason for using AI does not disappear. Some employees may simply find another way to access it.

This is where the real problem begins. A company may successfully block an application on its office network while remaining unaware that employees are using the same application through personal phones, private accounts or other connections.

Banning AI may restrict access through official systems, but it does not necessarily stop its use. In some situations, it can move that use beyond the organisation's visibility.

The use of AI at work is growing faster than many organisations can introduce their own systems and policies.

Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index reported that 75% of global knowledge workers were using AI at work. Among those using AI, 78% were bringing their own AI tools to work, commonly described as Bring Your Own AI (BYOAI).

This pattern aligns with broader enterprise trends. Research from Gartner shows that over 41% of employees actively acquire, modify, or use technology outside the visibility of IT department.

These figures are important because they show that employees are not waiting for their organisations to introduce every tool they want to use. But they should be understood carefully: they show workplace AI adoption and the use of personal tools; they do not prove that corporate bans are the reason employees use them.

The reasons can be practical. A legal associate may want to understand a long agreement more quickly. A researcher may need to organise a large amount of information. A software engineer may want help finding an error in code. An employee preparing a presentation may use AI to create an initial draft.

In each case, the employee is trying to save time or complete a task more efficiently.

This does not make every use acceptable. Employees still have a responsibility to follow workplace policies and protect confidential information. But organisations also need to understand why employees are turning to tools that have not been approved.

A policy that only says "do not use AI" may not answer the questions employees face every day: Which tools can I use? What information can I share? What should I do when the approved system cannot handle my task?

When these questions remain unanswered, employees may make their own decisions. That is how a technology policy can become disconnected from actual workplace behaviour.

In April 2023, Samsung Electronics reportedly faced incidents in which employees entered sensitive internal information into ChatGPT. Reports described employees sharing semiconductor source code and internal meeting information while using the tool for work-related tasks.

The incident became an important warning for companies considering the use of public AI platforms. It showed that sensitive information can leave an organisation through an ordinary workplace activity. An employee does not need to hack a system or deliberately attack a company. Copying information into an external chatbot can itself create a serious exposure.

Samsung's response included restrictions on generative AI use. The incident demonstrates why companies became concerned about employees using public AI tools. It does not, by itself, prove that bans push employees towards personal devices. That is a separate issue that organisations need to examine through evidence about employee behaviour.

There is another important point here. When information is entered into an external AI service, the organisation needs to understand the service's data practices.

Different AI providers have different terms and settings. Some services may use submitted content for model improvement under certain conditions, while others offer business arrangements with different data-retention and training terms. It would be incorrect to assume that every public AI service handles every prompt in the same way.

The concern is that employees using personal accounts may not know which terms apply to their information. The organisation may also have no contract, security review or clear process through which it can manage that risk.

For companies and legal institutions, Shadow AI is not just an IT concern. It can affect confidential information, legal responsibilities, customer trust and business interests.

1.⁠ ⁠Confidentiality and Attorney-Client Privilege

Legal professionals regularly work with sensitive information. This includes client communications, draft agreements, litigation strategies, personal records and documents that have not been made public.

Uploading such material to an external AI service without proper approval can create serious confidentiality concerns.

However, it is important to distinguish confidentiality from attorney-client privilege. Sharing privileged information with a third-party service does not automatically waive privilege in every situation. The legal result depends on the jurisdiction, the circumstances of disclosure, the service provider's access and the steps taken to maintain confidentiality.

Even where privilege is not automatically lost, sharing client information without proper safeguards may raise professional, contractual or ethical concerns.

For a law firm, the question should therefore not be limited to whether an AI tool gives a useful answer. It should also ask whether the information being shared is permitted to leave the firm's controlled environment.

2.⁠ ⁠Data Protection and Financial Penalties

The risk becomes more serious when employees share personal information through unapproved AI tools.

For example, a document may contain a client's name, address, financial details, identification information or other personal data. If that information is sent to an external service without appropriate safeguards, the organisation may face data-protection questions.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for penalties for specified failures. Under its Schedule, failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore. This does not mean that every employee's use of an AI chatbot automatically leads to that penalty. The relevant legal duties, facts and circumstances must be considered.

Similarly, under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), certain serious infringements can attract fines of up to €20 million or 4% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

These figures show why organisations need to take the handling of personal information seriously. But financial penalties are only one part of the problem. A data incident can also affect customer confidence, business relationships and the organisation's reputation.

IBM's 2023 Cost of a Data Breach Report estimated the global average cost of a data breach at $4.45 million. This is a figure from the 2023 report, not a current estimate specifically for Shadow AI incidents. It nevertheless gives an idea of the financial impact that data breaches can have on organisations.

Companies often hold information that gives them an advantage over competitors. It may include source code, product designs, pricing strategies, financial models, customer information or future business plans.

Keeping such information confidential is an important part of protecting trade secrets.

If employees regularly enter this material into public AI tools without checking the provider's terms or the organisation's security arrangements, the company may weaken its ability to show that it took reasonable steps to protect the information.

The legal position will depend on the relevant law and circumstances. But the business concern is simple: information that was meant to remain inside the organisation may be shared with an external service without proper control.

Blocking AI websites may appear to be the easiest response. A company can restrict access through its network, issue a policy and warn employees against using unapproved tools.

But consider the earlier example of the junior associate. Blocking a website on a company laptop does not prevent the associate from opening the same website on a personal phone. A personal hotspot can also take the activity outside the company's network.

The organisation may see that its office systems are following the policy. It may not see what is happening elsewhere.

This creates a difference between controlling access and controlling actual use.

A company that provides approved AI tools can set rules about who can use them, what information can be shared and which security measures apply. It can also review usage through appropriate technical controls.

By contrast, when employees use personal accounts and devices, the organisation may lose access to important information about that activity. It may not know which tools are being used, what information has been shared or whether an incident has taken place.

This does not mean companies should allow every AI tool. Some uses should remain prohibited, especially where sensitive information cannot be adequately protected. But treating a ban as the complete solution overlooks the reasons employees may continue using AI.

The issue is not simply whether an organisation permits or prohibits AI. It is whether its policy gives employees a safe and practical way to complete their work.

Companies need a system that protects information without ignoring the way employees actually work. This does not require unrestricted AI access. It requires clear rules, suitable tools and safeguards that match the sensitivity of the information.

1.⁠ ⁠Provide Approved Enterprise AI Tools

If employees are using public AI tools because they need help with everyday tasks, organisations should consider providing approved alternatives.

Enterprise AI services may offer different contractual and technical protections, including limits on data retention and commitments about whether customer inputs are used for model training. Some providers also offer Zero Data Retention (ZDR) arrangements.

The aim is to give employees a reliable tool for their daily work without making them depend on personal accounts or unapproved services.

2.⁠ ⁠Use Local AI Models for Highly Sensitive Information

Some work involves information that should not be sent to an external AI service. This may include sensitive source code, confidential legal strategy, certain client documents or important business information.

For such work, organisations can consider running AI models on their own infrastructure or within a controlled private environment.

Open-source model families such as Llama and Mistral may be considered for internal deployment, depending on the organisation's technical needs and resources. For particularly sensitive work, a disconnected or air-gapped system may offer an additional layer of protection.

But local deployment is not automatically safe. The organisation still needs to manage access, system security, updates and the information employees enter into the model.

3.⁠ ⁠Create a Clear Data Classification System

Employees should not have to guess whether a document can be shared with an AI tool. Organisations need to make these rules clear so that employees can understand what information is safe to share and what needs protection.

One practical way to do this is dividing information into three categories: public, internal and condidential.

Public information, such as published reports, press releases, and public case laws, can be used with apporved public or enterprise AI tools. Internal information, including routine meeting notes and general internal dragts, should only be used with AI tools approved under company policy. Confidential information, such as client records, personal data, contracts, source code and M&A information, requries greater care. Employees should use restricted tools or seek additional approval before sharing them.

This system should be easy to understand and connected to the organisation's existing confidentiality rules. Legal teams may need additional restrictions for privileged communications, litigation material and client documents.

Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools can help organisations identify and control the sharing of sensitive information.

For example, these tools can detect personal indentification numbers, financial details or confidential information in data being sent to external AI services. Depending on how the system works, it may block the request, flag it for review or remove senstive information before it reaches an external service.

These tools are not perfect. They may miss information or flag material that is harmless. They should therefore support, rather than replace, clear policies and employee awareness.

Even a well-designed policy can fail if employees do not understand how to follow it in their daily work.

Organisations should explain which AI tools are approved, what information must not be shared, when human review is required and how employees can request access to a new tool.

They should also create a simple way for employees to report accidental disclosure. If people are afraid to report mistakes, organisations may learn about incidents too late to respond effectively.

At the same time, employees must remain responsible for following the rules. Practical alternatives do not remove the duty to protect confidential information. Organisations need both clear expectations and fair accountability.

Shadow AI is not going to disappear simply because an organisation blocks access to certain AI tools. Employees still have deadlines, daily tasks and work to complete. When approved tools are unavailable or difficult to use, some may look for other ways to get the same work done.

This creates a problem for organisations. They may have rules against using unapproved AI services, but those rules do not necessarily tell them where employees are actually using AI or what information they are sharing.

This does not mean employees should be free to use any tool they want. Confidential information still needs protection, and employees must take responsibility for how they use AI. But organisations also need to look at why employees are turning to tools outside the approved system.

If a tool is helping employees complete routine work more easily, the organisation should consider whether it can provide a safe alternative. It should also make clear what information can be shared and where approval is required.

The real issue is not just whether employees are following AI policies. It is whether those policies work in the way people actually do their jobs. If organisations want to manage Shadow AI, they need to understand its use rather than simply try to stop it.

The Convenience Trap: When Techonology Starts Making Decisions For Us

#9684. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9682. Lightweight C++ CSPRNG Implementation for Custom Schnorr Zero-Knowledge Proofs Without Heavy Libraries

Evaluating the cryptographic soundness of a custom Schnorr zero-knowledge proof implementation requires examining how data flows from raw entropy generation through commitment binding, Fiat-Shamir challenge derivation, and final scalar validation. In educational repositories such as dev-dawud/ZeroKnowledgeProof, the core vulnerability rarely stems from syntax errors, but rather from the silent breakdown of mathematical assumptions when low-level primitives are poorly constructed.

The foundation of any Schnorr protocol rests on the ephemeral nonce k. When a prover generates a commitment R = gk mod p, the security of the private key x depends entirely on the unpredictability of k. If k is sourced from a non-cryptographic pseudo-random number generator like std::mt19937 or rand(), the internal linear recurrence register or Mersenne state is seeded by a predictable 32-bit system timestamp. An observer capturing multiple proof transcripts can reconstruct the internal state, predict future k values prior to proof execution, and compute the private key via x = (s - k) \cdot c-1 mod q. The algebraic hardness assumption collapses because predictable entropy turns a one-way mathematical trapdoor into a solvable linear equation.

Moving from an interactive protocol to a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof introduces the Fiat-Shamir heuristic, which transforms the verifier's random challenge into a hash of the transcript: c = H(R || Y || m). A structural flaw frequently observed in custom implementations is incomplete transcript binding. If the developer omits either the public key Y or the commitment R from the hash preimage, the binding mechanism fails. An attacker can manipulate the hash inputs to forge a valid response s for an arbitrary statement without possessing the discrete logarithm. The hash function acts as a cryptographic accumulator; omitting components breaks its ability to cryptographically tie the prover's ephemeral state to the exact verification key.

Response validation further exposes the implementation to modulo bias. The response calculation s = k + c \cdot x mod q requires mapping raw random byte arrays into finite field scalars. A naive modulo reduction (bytes mod q) introduces statistical skew because the input byte space (such as 2256) is not an exact multiple of the curve order q. Lower numerical values occur with a marginally higher probability, concentrating the distribution of k over thousands of test proofs. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

#9678. 5 Costco Baked Goods To Buy And 4 To Skip

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The holidays are just around the corner. Between Thanksgiving and Christmas, you'll have Friendsgivings, work parties, school functions, and every other conceivable event that may require you to bring a baked good. Sometimes, it's a bit too much, which is why there's absolutely no shame in going the store-bought route instead of firing up the oven at home.

Prices are as of the date of publication and may vary based on region.

Costco is a godsend if you're hosting a large group for brunch. There are a handful of breakfast-centric items on this list, but first and foremost are the bagels. I snagged a bag of the plain bagels, but Costco has several other flavors, including Parmesan Cheese and the new Pretzel Bagels.

An 8-pack of Plain Bagels retails for $5.66, an unsurprisingly great value given the store. True to form, the bagels are also quite large, making them worthy of a full meal on their own. While they don't come pre-sliced, I prefer to buy bagels whole as it helps keep them fresh. Each bagel is soft, chewy, and toasts up perfectly.

If bagels are the main focus of your meal, there's no need to overthink things. Costco bagels are great, even if they don't come from a shop focused entirely on them. This is the perfect, no-stress addition to any breakfast and a definite freezer staple.

Because our relationship is built on trust, I'm going to come right out and say the "skips" on this list aren't hard passes, but more likely items you can survive without. Frankly, Costco doesn't make many bad products, and the Buttermilk Biscuits are one such example.

These things are huge. I honestly don't think I've ever seen a biscuit this large, let alone ten of them for $7.93. I'll jump into the review in a moment, but the reason the biscuits landed in my skip pile is that they're one of the few baked goods I purchased that came with cooking instructions and the only one that I think really needs to be cooked to be properly enjoyed.

A cold biscuit is, in my opinion, a sad biscuit, and while Costco's Buttermilk Biscuits are serviceable at room temperature, they're worlds better when warmed up. You can toss them in the oven or do what I did and zap each one in the microwave for about 30 seconds. The result is a steaming, fluffy, buttery biscuit roughly the size of a baseball. These are really good biscuits, but if they need to be warm to really enjoy them, there are more convenient options in the Costco bakery.

France has delivered a lot of wonderful things to the United States — looking at you, Lady Liberty — but the best cultural exchange may have been the croissant. Almost impossibly airy, flaky, and absurdly buttery, the croissant is a hugely versatile pastry. It can go sweet, it can go savory, or you can just munch on one as a snack.

A 12-pack of Costco Croissants is just $6.80. For comparison, my local Target has an 8-pack of Pillsbury Original Crescent Rolls for $3.39. Don't get me wrong, I love those fresh-baked little bundles of joy, but a single Costco croissant is equivalent to multiple of the smaller home-baked ones. The value is unbeatable, and the flavor is close behind. These croissants are everything you could hope for, and, thanks to their size, you can really get creative with them. Slice one in half and make a sandwich or, as I did, take 8 and put them into a fantastic French toast bake. It's culinary cultural inception and a great way to use a very tasty baked good.

Costco's muffins have a long and surprisingly winding history filled with recipe and size changes that bordered on national scandals. Thankfully, it seems that the muffins have once again found their sweet spot as some of the better options from the Costco bakery. Of course, this is a skip, though, so while I enjoy the Vanilla Chocolate Chip Muffins (which retail for $7.93 for an 8-count package), you can do better.

Costco has a number of different muffin flavors. Blueberry, Vanilla Chocolate Chip, and Double Chocolate are the standard options, but seasonal and rotating offerings include everything from Blueberry Creme to Pumpkin Streusel. I've reviewed Costco's Double Chocolate Muffins before and they're fantastic; rich, filled with chocolate, and riding that fine line between a breakfast pastry and a dessert.

The Vanilla Chocolate Chip Muffins are plenty tasty in their own right. Each one is remarkably soft and spongy, with a sweetness that makes it taste like a supersized Little Debbie treat. The chocolate chips are large, but not super evenly distributed. These are perfectly serviceable muffins you're almost guaranteed to enjoy, but Costco has better muffins, so these are an easy skip.

Let's start with the fact that this pack has not one, but two coconut-based bars. The Wildberry Macaroons are admittedly tasty thanks to a tart berry jam that rests between a bevy of toasted coconut flakes and a soft, buttery macaroon base. Yes, that's double coconut in one bar, but a single, good coconut option is just fine by me. The issue is that the Macaroon Madness Bars are a second coconut-based treat disguised as a blondie. Until I took a bite, I had no idea that this bar was also filled with coconut. It's not as good or as interesting as the Wildberry Macaroon, so this feels like a total waste of space.

The Artisan Rolls are sold in a 12-pack for $6.80. They're precut and, you guessed it, they're big. The ciabatta-style bread is chewy, airy, and perfect for sandwiches. Especially leftover sandwiches. Perhaps after a food-centric holiday. What I'm getting at is that you need to buy these for the day after Thanksgiving to make some spectacular, carbtastic, leftover sandwiches. They're hearty enough to handle whatever combination of turkey, gravy, potatoes, stuffing, and cranberry sauce you can throw at them, but not so dense that you'll fill up on bread. A good roll in the right setting can make a meal, and Costco's Artisan Rolls are perfect for making the kind of sandwich that inevitably leads to a wonderful nap.

I've waxed poetic about Costco's portion sizes thus far because, for the most part, I can find a way to normalize a massive amount of baked goods in the right setting. There is an exception to every rule, though, and the baguette is mine.

Priced at $5.66 for a two-pack of baguettes, this is an almost absurd amount of bread. Each baguette is nearly two feet long. Combined, that's the height of a 6-year-old. Unlike some of the other items I tried, the baguette also seems to have the shortest shelf life. You either need to eat it that day or freeze it immediately to avoid the outer crust from becoming chewy. If you're hosting a spaghetti dinner that night, this is a decent enough option, but it's still a bread that simply doesn't stay good for long.

I'm not entirely out on the Costco Baguette, but beyond being generally impractical, it's not a product that blew me away with either taste or texture. It's fine, and with so many other things to choose from, fine isn't enough.

In the world of sweet breakfast pastries, I think the Danish is too often forgotten. It's basically the flaky, buttery goodness of a croissant paired with pie filling. Honestly, how could that combo ever be bad?

Costco's danishes come in packs of four. There are a few unique flavors to choose from, with Cheese, Cherry, and Almond as the standards, while seasonal favorites include Strawberry Cream Cheese and Apple Cinnamon. The mix-and-match portion of the name comes from the pricing: You can get two four-packs for $13.61, which is what I did to end up with a Cheese and an Apple.

True to form, these Danishes are hefty and really tasty. The fillings are sweet, but not overwhelmingly so, and the pastry portion is baked to perfection. The Cheese flavor is especially great for anyone who lives on the more savory side of the spectrum, but still likes to dabble in the occasional sweet treat. The Apple was my favorite, though. I like any excuse to eat a classic apple pie for breakfast, and Costco's Danish is the perfect one.

I purchased all nine Costco baked goods at the same time and brought them home to photograph and sample. My evaluations were based on flavor, texture, and overall value.

And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9667. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9660. Not American Or Cheddar: Grab This Cheese For Perfect Breakfast Sandwiches (Thanks, Martha Stewart)

Practical, budget-friendly, and endlessly versatile, sandwiches are an everyday staple for a reason. Though there's no right or one way to do them, certain combinations have proven to be instant crowd-pleasers. Enter the humble bacon, egg, and cheese, the breakfast of champions and Bobby Flay's favorite late-night snack. It sounds simple enough, but the ingredients you use and how you treat them can be the difference between standard deli fare and Michelin-worthy grub. If you like the sound of the latter option, borrow a tip from the icon herself, Martha Stewart, and use fontina cheese next time you're making one.

Fontina is a must-try Italian cheese. Originating from the Aosta Valley in the Italian Alps, it's a semi-soft cow's milk cheese that's been produced since the 12th century. Its high fat content is responsible for its creamy texture, accompanied by a mild nutty and earthy flavor that intensifies with age. Beyond these already impressive attributes, the thing that makes it so well-suited to a bacon, egg, and cheese is its melting capability. You'll have no trouble finding it in Italian dishes like fonduta alla Valdostana (Italy's answer to fondue) and polenta concia, where it's melted down into a thick, gooey consistency with polenta, milk, and butter. Martha Stewart also pairs fontina with pizza on a pie that features lemon and rosemary (via YouTube).

There are many versions of fontina available, but for the most traditional, pick up Fontina DOP, which is made from raw, whole milk of native Valdostana cattle breeds fed on alpine grass or hay. Because it uses raw milk, it must be aged past the USDA's required 60 days. To put it all together, take a cue from Martha Stewart and use an English muffin as your base. Toast it until golden, then layer on crispy bacon and eggs cooked to your liking. While the eggs are still hot, add a slice or two of fontina and let the residual heat melt the cheese into a creamy, gooey layer.

A bacon, egg, and cheese paired with fontina is already a winning combination, but there are a few ways to make it even better. For quick melting and an extra hit of creamy flavor, place the fontina on your bread and give it a blast under the broiler. You can also pop your bacon under there to get it extra crispy, but hold off on adding the egg until afterward. It's delicate, after all, and can quickly overcook under such intense heat. On that note, keep a close eye on your cheese as it broils — there's a fine line between beautifully melted and golden and burnt beyond saving.

Beyond breakfast sandwiches, you can also use fontina to make another classic: grilled cheese. Given its excellent reputation for meltability, adding fontina to a grilled cheese is practically a no-brainer. You don't have to stop at bread and cheese, either. If you want to put a twist on the classic grilled cheese and tomato soup pairing, tuck in a few slices of tomato and some fresh basil leaves.

In a nod to its Italian heritage, fontina is also a welcome addition to a panini. Your idea of a panini might depend on where you are in the world. In Italy, panino simply means sandwich, and often features a more restrained combination of cured meats, cheese, and vegetables than its U.S. counterpart. So if you want the fontina to shine, take a little inspiration from its homeland. Try layering it with thinly sliced prosciutto, roasted red peppers, and a few leaves of peppery arugula on ciabatta. Add a drizzle of olive oil and a little freshly cracked black pepper and sea salt, then use a panini press until the bread is crisp and the cheese has melted.
