#9613. 10 Protein-Packed Substitutes For Mayo In Chicken Salad

Chicken salad is like edible Americana, a comfort food that's beloved for its taste, nutrition, and versatility. You can find it in the prepared section of your local supermarket or on the menu of your favorite diner. Trying to cut down on carbohydrates? Have a scoop on a salad. Want a light and easy lunch? Have it as a club or between two pieces of toasted whole-grain bread. More importantly, though, chicken salad is like a ball of clay ready to be shaped by your taste preferences. You can take it in infinite directions: Mediterranean, Southwest, Spanish, French, Indian, Vietnamese. Have some extra sprigs of cilantro or half a bag of red grapes lying hanging around the fridge? Add 'em. Don't know what to do with those leftover pecans or knob of fresh ginger? You can throw those in, too.

But the foundation of any respectable chicken salad is its creamy binder. In that regard, mayonnaise is the undisputed classic, turning your basic diced chicken breast into something moist, savory, and luscious. However, plenty of other ingredients deliver that signature smoothness — just with more protein. From tzatziki to silken tofu to labneh, there are tons of options that deliver both texture and an added pop of flavor. Whether you're minding your macros or just looking for a new spin on a classic dish, this list of protein-packed mayo substitutes is for you.

Yogurt has a long and storied reputation as a health food, so long, in fact, that its beneficial properties are documented in Indian Ayurvedic medicinal writings from more than 7,000 years ago. Today, it's seen as a better-for-you breakfast option, loaded with beneficial probiotics, calcium, and, of course, protein. Yogurt, especially the more thoroughly strained Greek variety, has an excellent calorie-to-protein ratio (about 16 grams of protein per 150 calories when made with whole milk), which is why it has become so popular with bodybuilders and wellness influencers.

However, Greek yogurt still has a place in ordinary kitchens, and it's especially useful for people looking for a healthier alternative to mayonnaise, cream cheese, or any other creamy, high-fat, high-cholesterol product, which is why it makes such a great addition to homemade chicken salad. Even when prepared with mayonnaise, chicken salad is a relatively nutritious lunch option, typically made with low-fat chicken breast, fresh herbs, diced veggies, and maybe some nuts or sliced grapes. Whole milk yogurt, which is creamier than low-fat options, builds on that by adding extra protein, moisture, and the richness synonymous with a good chicken salad. It also adds a little tang that complements the subdued nature of poultry and plays well with other common chicken-salad additions, like mustard, dill, or curry powder.

It feels like every week there's another article or study being published identifying the benefits of gut health. This increased focus on the gut microbiome and the trillions of microorganisms that occupy it has brought all sorts of fermented dairy products, which are packed with probiotics and other useful bacteria, back into the nutritional spotlight. In this department, Greek yogurt is king (at least in the United States), but other styles are slowly making their way to the supermarket dairy aisle. One of them is skyr, also known as Icelandic yogurt.

Technically classified as a cheese because its proteins are coagulated with rennet (a naturally occurring enzyme), skyr is dense, almost custard-like, with a mild sweetness and less assertive bite than Greek yogurt. Nutritionally, the two dairy products have an almost identical profile, although skyr is typically slightly higher in protein per serving due to a more rigorous straining process. But it's that straining — and subsequent thicker texture — that makes skyr such a terrific mayo substitute, delivering the same full creaminess without the more forward lactic tang of typical yogurt. How you use it in your chicken salad is a personal preference. If you like your chicken salad on the more unctuous side, use it as is; if you like it a little looser, thin your skyr with a tablespoon or two of milk, which may also help coat each ingredient more evenly.

On a per-calorie basis, cottage cheese is hard to beat among high-protein foods, with (on average) 12-14 grams of protein per 100-calorie serving. Unlike yogurt, which is fermented with bacteria, cottage cheese is made through acidification. As milk becomes more acidic and the pH level drops, the proteins denature, clump, and coagulate into tiny little curds. Although the process is simple, there's a lot of variability between brands. Some are saltier or creamier or contain larger curds.

But the most influential factor, especially regarding your chicken salad, is the fat content. While low-fat cottage cheese has fewer calories per serving, it lacks the richness needed to rehydrate dry chicken. Beyond extra unctuousness, full-fat cottage cheese adds salinity, clean milky notes, and a very mild cheese flavor. However, there's one major difference between cottage cheese and mayonnaise: Texture. Straight out of the plastic tub, cottage cheese can be, well, lumpy. This may not bother you in the slightest, but if it does, there's an easy workaround: Whipping the cottage cheese. You can do this with a hand mixer, mini food processor, or even just a big fork; the goal being to break those curds into a finer texture similar to ricotta. You can use the same technique to incorporate this high-protein food into smoothies, dips, and even macaroni and cheese.

Hummus was the "it" food product of the early 2000s, but in the years since, it has faded in popularity. Maybe we were just given too much, too fast: Beet hummus, carrot hummus, lentil hummus, chocolate hummus — each variation obfuscating the beauty of this simple, timeless, life-sustaining food. Hummus, the type made from chickpeas, sesame paste (tahini), and olive oil, is an ancient form of plant-based protein foundational to Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines. When blended, the ingredients make a velvety emulsion that — depending on how much ice water or oil you use — can be spread or scooped over everything, from bulgur wheat to falafel wraps.

It's also a great addition to salads — including ones made from chicken. Here, hummus provides an extra protein boost as well as some much-needed fattiness. Its blend of Middle Eastern spices — cumin, sumac, garlic, za'atar — contributes a warmth and brightness that cuts through the inherent blandness of cooked chicken breast. If using hummus as the foundation of your chicken salad, consider adding other Mediterranean ingredients, like capers, olives, walnuts, almonds, fresh tomato, or cucumbers. You can use your favorite supermarket brand, or just quickly whip up delicious hummus at home.

Probably the most underrated ingredient on this list, silken tofu is a centuries-old, plant-based protein with limitless applications. Like other forms of bean curd, silken tofu is made from soybeans, but it's worlds different from soft, medium, or firm varieties. While it comes in similar packaging, silken tofu is hardly solid; it's more like a pudding or flan that will fall apart if you try to pick it up with a fork. However, it's precisely this loose creaminess that makes silken tofu such a terrific substitute for mayonnaise in your next chicken salad.

Besides being a great protein source — containing around 20 grams per 16-ounce package — silken tofu can easily be made smooth and pourable. When blended, it becomes something akin to Alfredo sauce, with a velvety consistency that's ideal for coating chicken. Another advantage of silken tofu is its taste — or lack thereof. You're dealing with a blank canvas here, one that will quickly absorb whatever seasonings, herbs, or sauces you mix with it. It may need some doctoring to get the texture right, but just use this as another opportunity to add flavor. Try adding cilantro and lime, tarragon and sherry vinegar, or hot sauce, for a Buffalo wing-inspired chicken salad.

There are only so many ways to add creaminess to food without relying on dairy, a fatty emulsion, or some complicated form of food chemistry. Adding a can of blended beans is one of them. Legumes, like black beans, kidney beans, and butter beans, have a starchy center that turns smooth and pillowy when blended. Most commercial varieties you find at your typical supermarket are good for cooking, but some have a more distinct flavor than others.

When making chicken salad, it's best to use beans with a clean, neat taste and not too much earthiness. For this, white, cannellini, or Great Northern beans are best. They won't overwhelm the other ingredients in your chicken salad, but they also aren't entirely neutral-tasting, either. The key to using these legumes is to purée them with different spices, herbs, and condiments, like Worcestershire sauce, miso, or a splash of vinegar. To achieve a texture that's similar to mayonnaise, you'll likely need to add some liquid or fat. Olive or another neutral oil works, but adding a heavily seasoned broth will give you an even better result. To do this, make a quick pan sauce with sautéed aromatics, seasonings, and stock; add it to your beans, then blend everything in a blender or food processor.

This one is a little sneaky. Egg yolks are inherently fatty, but they also contain natural emulsifiers that turn into a creamy paste when blended. That means you don't have to add a drop of mayonnaise (which, ironically, is made predominantly from egg yolks) to achieve a luscious texture. But egg salad brings more to the party than just creaminess. If you've ever watched a TikTok nutritionist worth their creatine, then you're probably frustratingly aware that egg whites are one of nature's purest protein sources.

This combination of smooth, fatty yolk and protein-rich white makes egg salad an incredible substitute for mayo. It's a tongue-in-cheek pairing, for sure, but this whimsical culinary mashup also delivers on taste. Because eggs are a tad sulfurous on their own, season them generously with ingredients like Dijon mustard, capers, lemon juice, smoked paprika, or even a few shakes of curry powder. However, the key to achieving a natural creaminess is proper egg cookery, which essentially boils down to not overcooking your hard-boiled eggs. The answer: A quick dunk in the ice bath for about 10-15 minutes to halt cooking and preserve those fluffy yolks.

Want the nutritional upside of yogurt with an added burst of refreshing Mediterranean flavors? Sounds like it's tzatziki time. The yogurt-based dip is most closely associated with Greek cuisine, serving as a cooling counterpoint to robustly seasoned grilled meats, fried zucchini, and platters of pita. And, while its protein content isn't on the same level as skyr or cottage cheese, it isn't negligible, either, which is why it's another smart mayo substitute for your next chicken salad.

Tzatziki looks simple, but it delivers a chorus of complex flavors that few condiments can match. It's all things smooth, rich, tangy, and fresh, thanks to a blend of fresh herbs and other aromatics. Besides yogurt, the predominant ingredient is cucumber. Paired with fresh mint, dill, and garlic, this creates a clean, powerful taste profile. It instantly elevates ordinary chicken into something moist and tender. Slip your tzatziki-coated chicken salad into a pita and top with shredded lettuce, tomato, black olives, and sliced red onion for a memorable lunch. While tzatziki is popular, it can be difficult to find good options in your average supermarket. Thankfully, a quality tzatziki sauce is easy to put together; just remember to squeeze the moisture out of your cucumbers. Otherwise, your sauce will be too wet and separate.

Labneh is made by straining Greek yogurt in cheesecloth until you remove the remaining liquid whey. This not only creates a denser product, but it also concentrates the flavor. It's traditionally made with goat's milk, which is a little grassy on the palate and has a slightly tangier finish than a cow's milk cheese or yogurt. Unlike yogurt, though, which you typically eat with a spoon, labneh is more of a dip, perfect for crudités, pita, lavash, or even grilled fruits. It has a decadent mouthfeel and is decidedly more savory, especially when dressed with olive oil, making it a nice way to rejuvenate an otherwise tired chicken salad.

But there's no reason to pigeonhole this spreadable yogurt as savory or sweet; it works beautifully with both taste profiles. You can roll it in za'atar, sumac, and fresh mint, or crust it with pistachios and drizzle it with honey. Since it's the thickest yogurt-based product on this list, when using it for chicken salad, you'll likely want to add a splash of milk or a non-dairy alternative to loosen it up. If you can't find labneh in stores, you can literally just add Greek yogurt to a cheesecloth, hang it above your sink, and let it drip for a few hours until it's firm and extra creamy.

Like most dairy products, feta is a solid protein source, with about 4 grams per 2-ounce serving; however, it differs from other cheeses because it's brined in a salt-water and whey solution rather than traditionally aged. This process helps preserve the cheese while also imbuing it with its signature salinity. If you've been lucky enough to try quality feta, you know that this soft, crumbly cheese packs a punch. In the mouth, it has a clean, fresh cream flavor and mild tang, making it a natural partner for grilled meats like beef, lamb, or chicken.

Feta isn't spreadable, nor does it melt, but you can easily transform its texture by dropping a few chunks into a blender or food processor and "whipping" it until smooth. The result is smooth, salty, and spoonable — and perfect for chicken salad. When using whipped feta, consider both its salt content and mild acidic bite. These are strong flavors that should be balanced with other sweet and savory ingredients. Try pairing it with starchy, nutty, or mildly sweet foods like roasted butternut squash, pistachios, dried cranberries, or nectarines.

#9612. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9610. Forget Apple Pie: An Easier Thanksgiving Dessert Bobby Flay Recommends

While turkey and stuffing may be the centerpieces on a Thanksgiving table during the main course, almost everyone knows that the meal isn't complete without a sweet finish. And no other type of dessert is more appropriate for this holiday than pie, including one filled with tender, sweet apples. While you can get top-ranking apple pies from a grocery store, making your own can feel much more satisfying and give you bragging rights. However, assembling one from scratch can be an ordeal. Luckily, chef Bobby Flay has a much easier solution: Make a crostata instead.

A crostata is a type of Italian tart that is traditionally made with pasta frolla, a dough whose ingredients typically include flour, sugar, butter, and eggs, although recipes can differ. It's a versatile dessert that can have many different fillings, including one containing ricotta that's one of Rick Steves' favorite desserts in Italy. The form of a crostata is equally varied, as it can be made in a tart pan or free-form, and it's this latter style that Flay prefers.

In an Instagram post, Flay shared, "My tarts, pies and cakes are going to have that 'rustic' look no matter what ... a [crostata] is supposed to feel that way so it's my go-to move!" And if you feel the same way, you should give this dessert a spin. The biggest advantage it has over a traditional pie is its simplicity. All you need to do is place the dough on a baking sheet, add your apples to the center, and fold up the crust over the edges of the filling to hold everything together. Your dough doesn't even need to be a perfect circle, and there's no need for a top crust.

A crostata is simpler to make than many pies, but there's still a little bit of technique and preparation involved in assembling one. While pasta frolla is the traditional crust, you're not bound to using it, and even your favorite all-purpose pie crust recipe can work to bake a rustic apple crostata for Thanksgiving. You can also opt to use premade pie crust from the supermarket if making it from scratch is a little too time-consuming, especially if you have a litany of other dishes to prepare for the holiday. When assembling your crostata, you want to make sure that your crust remains cold but is still pliable.

Now comes time for the filling. Since a crostata is a flatter riff on a pie, you'll want to make sure to thinly slice your apples and not make a huge mound — about 2 inches high is enough. Also, make sure to leave about a 2-inch border between the filling and the edge to give you enough crust to fold over your apples, and create some rough pleats here and there to help contain the filling. Remember that the look of this bake is rustic, so nothing needs to be perfect.

You can also add other things to your crostata filling to give it a little extra pizzazz, including cranberries, golden raisins, or walnuts. Seasonings like Chinese five-spice can add layers of dimension to your rustic apple crostata, too, and a little liqueur can take this dessert to the next level. You can also replace the apples with other fruits, including pears, to bring an unexpected element to the Thanksgiving table.

#9608. Do You Compare Yourself to Your Partner? It’s Not All Bad

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

After venturing through the wasteland of modern dating, it would be natural to harbor disdain for social comparison. Dating apps require you to stand out, which means you can’t just be yourself; you need to sell yourself as more appealing than the 50,000 sexy singles in your area. Putting yourself on display and knowing you’re being compared to others can feel exhausting. But once you’ve swiped right, matched, and established a lasting romantic relationship, surely the social comparisons are all in the rearview mirror…right?

That couldn’t be further from the truth. Research suggests we compare ourselves to romantic partners more than anyone else in our lives—on average several times per day. In my own studies, I’ve endeavored to unpack these daily partner comparisons to understand: What kinds of people make partner comparisons, and why? The answer, it seems, depends on the type of comparisons partners are making: either based on our unique abilities, or on the opinions we hold. The good news: Comparisons can offer a learning opportunity and even bring us closer together as partners.

Many partner comparisons revolve around who is better at a given activity—also known as “ability-based comparisons.” These comparisons can range from trivial (Who’s the better bowler?) to weighty (Who’s the better parent?).

In my latest study with collaborators Robin Edelstein and Stephen Garcia, we studied patterns in who makes more of these ability-based comparisons. We surveyed over 1,100 U.S. adults in romantic relationships, asking them questions about how regularly they compare themselves to their partners. For instance, one question asked them, “To what extent do you pay a lot of attention to how you do things relative to how your significant other does things?” Participants also completed measures of self-esteem, relationship quality, and demographics.

The results were clear: People who were younger, those with lower self-esteem, and those in shorter and less satisfying relationships were particularly likely to make ability-based comparisons. Men in relationships with men also reported making more of these comparisons than any other gender pairing, but we only surveyed 37 men in same-gender relationships, so take this finding with a grain of salt.

A second type of comparison involves comparing judgments and attitudes—known as “opinion-based comparisons.” In these comparisons, people evaluate their own opinions by comparing with those of their partners. For instance, before enthusiastically locking in a major purchase, a partner might wonder, “Would my partner consider this a good deal, too?” Similar considerations may arise in the contexts of voting, child care, or anywhere judgments lead to decisions.

When it came to who was most prone to making opinion-based comparisons, our results flipped: These were most common among people in longer and more satisfying relationships.

Taken together, these individual characteristics paint two portraits of people who frequently compare themselves to their partners.

The first portrait is that of a young, insecure partner who is in a newer relationship and unsure whether that relationship will work out. Think Bella Swan from Twilight who worries endlessly about whether Edward is too good for her. And, indeed, when we asked participants why they made partner comparisons, two of their motives included assessing equity and predicting the relationship’s trajectory. For instance, participants grappled with questions like, “Am I doing for her as she is doing for me?”

The second portrait is that of someone in a long-term relationship who respects the knowledge and expertise of their partner and seeks to harness it as a tool for growth and decision making. For this one, think Leslie Knope from Parks and Rec who regularly compares her own judgments to those of her long-term work wife, Ann Perkins, as a means to make better decisions. This theme, too, emerged from our participants. For instance, one participant lovingly wrote about how his partner outshines him in most areas, and this dynamic continually inspires him to grow.

Yet partner comparison isn’t limited to these two portraits. Whereas these portraits describe those who compare most frequently, we found most people make some comparisons sometimes. What motivates occasional comparers?

The two most common motives for partner comparison were striving to gain a deeper understanding of oneself and one’s partner. With respect to self-evaluation, one participant shared that they compare regularly to their partner because comparison helps them benchmark their progress toward goals. Want to know if your cooking class has paid off? One of the best ways to evaluate your growth is to see if your latest dish can delight your family in the same way that your partner’s cooking always does.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Partner comparisons can also help us understand our partners’ quirks, what we call partner evaluation. For instance, one participant shared how she compares her upbringing to that of her partner, which helps her understand why her partner thinks, feels, and behaves so differently than she does.

It’s no secret that social comparison can sting. No parent wants to hear, “I like Mom better,” and no newlywed wants to hear, “How did you land such a catch?” We find in our studies that partner comparisons are often involuntarily thrust upon people who would have preferred not to be compared. It can be true what they say, “Comparison is the thief of joy.”

But comparison does more than push our emotional buttons. Partner comparisons help us assess our relationship and calibrate our behavior, such as how we divide household labor. They allow us to make important decisions, like who should take ownership over responsibilities. They serve as sources of growth, and they teach us about ourselves and our partners.

Comparing yourself to your partner isn’t necessarily a sign that something’s wrong. Rather, partner comparison can be a handy strategy for making sense of your social world. The key is to use it as a tool that stays in its place, rather than letting it undermine your self-worth or relationship.

Serena D’souza contributed to this article.

Zachary Reese, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of psychology at the University of San Francisco where he directs the Love and Communication Lab. He received his undergraduate degree in psychology from Goucher College in 2016 and his Ph.D. in social psychology from the University of Michigan in 2022.

#9607. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9604. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9603. How Your Imagination Can Work for You or Against You

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

I have a pretty vivid imagination, sometimes for the good, sometimes not. I love it when it helps me to create new stories or songs, or when I can daydream about fun times ahead. But it can also lead to fear or worry, like when I imagine something terrible befalling the people or places I love.

Is there some way to nurture the positive aspects of imagination while minimizing the problematic? According to Cassandra Vieten, director of research at the Arthur C. Clarke Center for Human Imagination, there is. In her new book, Imagine That, she explains imagination’s importance in our everyday lives—a way to understand our past, navigate the present, and explore future possibilities. If we learn more about its inner workings, she argues, we can use it more consciously and deliberately to create the kind of life we want.

“Imagination is something we all possess, something we can all practice, for free and with equal opportunity,” says Vieten. “When someone develops this capacity, they gain something almost magical: the ability to see multiple futures simultaneously and navigate toward the preferred ones.”

Many of us tend to conflate imagination with creativity, thinking that being able to imagine new ideas is the same as bringing them to fruition. While the two may indeed be related, this is far too limited a view of what imagination can be, writes Vieten.

“Imagination is an essential, foundational capacity that allows us to simulate reality and transcend it to explore possibilities beyond the known,” she says.

In our everyday lives, imagination is what helps us make predictions as well as come up with novel (or creative) ideas. For example, we might imagine how stopping for a coffee on our way to work will help us focus (simulation imagination, based on past experience). But we might also use our imagination to transcend what’s known and come up with a totally new innovation or product idea once we arrive at the office (generative imagination).

“Imagination weaves throughout the fabric of our cognitive, sensory, and relational lives—you are constantly speculating, visualizing, rehearsing, wondering,” she writes.

These types of imagination show up differently in the brain, writes Vieten. Simulation is primarily centered in the default mode network (DMN), a part of the brain that remains active when we aren’t engaging in a specific task. The DMN is where we tend to mull over future interactions, plans, or options, often subconsciously (or even unconsciously).

Generative imagination, on the other hand, comes by freeing ourselves from the DMN’s limitations (or, some would say, tyranny). If we can get out of the everyday chatter and let our minds truly wander freely around disparate parts of the brain, making new neural connections, we have a better chance of generating something truly unique.

“Rather than simulating or iterating, comparing and contrasting, generative imagination is focused on combining, reconfiguring, or transcending existing knowledge to generate novel outputs,” writes Vieten.

Either way, imagination isn’t frivolous, she writes; it’s important for our everyday functioning as well as creative self-expression. It helps us solve problems, while also expanding possibilities of what could be, giving us “the gift of wonder, whimsy, and surprise, the whoas and the wows of our lives,” she writes.

Imagination can sometimes be problematic, though. For example, we might imagine that our spouse is mad at us and worry about what might happen when she gets home from work when, actually, she’s not mad at all. This can cause us needless worry, not to mention potentially trigger a fight.

We can also imagine that other people are unpleasant or even dangerous based on untested biases. These can be formed in part via our imagination, which tries to prepare us for unknown encounters, often behind the scenes at an unconscious level.

“We regularly imagine entire narratives, scenes, and interactions without intending to or even knowing we’re doing it,” writes Vieten.

Our imagination is often busy filling in the missing parts of our memories and perceptions, which are by nature incomplete. Memories, rather than being etched in our minds, are recreated (and often changed) each time they’re recalled. Similarly, we can’t perceive everything at once, so our imagination completes the picture for us, adding interpretations, too. This means it’s easy to corrupt memories or miss details of a situation—which can sometimes lead to problems (think eyewitness accounts of crimes, for example).

Understanding these darker sides of imagination can help us tame them somewhat, says Vieten. “You can practice bringing greater attention to what you are imagining, recognize it as imagination, and decide whether it holds useful information, is irrelevant, or is actually causing harm.”

While the book covers the neuroscience behind imagination, it’s also about how to harness our imagination more effectively. Your personal imagination style may depend, in part, on your genetics (such as neurodiversity), culture, and life experiences. Understanding this can help you figure out where you might want to try moving the needle one way or the other.

To assess your own imaginative strengths and weaknesses, here are some key imagination modes Vieten outlines in her book.

1. Receptiveness. “How willing you are to imagine—and how receptive you are to whatever bubbles up.” If you are high in receptivity, you may find it easy to do guided visualizations, for example; if low in receptivity, you may be less willing to imagine unknown scenarios.

2. Presence. How much do you embody your imagined experiences? If you tend to be absorbed, immersed, and emotionally involved in imagined scenarios, you’re high in presence; if you tend to observe these imaginings from a distance, you’re less so.

3. Embellishment. “How vivid, detailed, and elaborate people make their imaginings.” Those high in embellishment can imagine intricate scenarios with much more detail, clarity, nuance, and complexity. Those low in embellishment might be more “big picture” folks, who may not be able to conjure up details as much.

4. Originality. How much your imagination is fueled by what is or could be, based on reality, versus how much it veers from that and is based more on fantasy and novelty.

5. Temporality. How much your imagination is associated with time (in other words, assessing the past or projecting into the future) versus how much it is agnostic around time (not based on any particular time). (Vieten admits the science on this mode is not completely settled, but says there appear to be some differences in how people engage with time while imagining.)

Each of these modes has pros and cons, she argues. For example, being high in receptivity may mean you’re more cognitively flexible and open to new experiences, but can also mean you’re overly compliant and easily manipulated. Similarly, the upside of being high in originality is that it can fuel advancements in art and science, though it can lead to boredom with everyday life.

Considering my own strengths and weaknesses, I noticed that I seem to be high in receptivity and embodiment, but low in embellishment and originality (and mixed when it comes to temporality). Recognizing this makes me think about paying more attention to details in my environment and playing around with more fantastical ideas, especially if I’m wanting to fuel my creativity.

To that end, Vieten provides avenues for stretching our imagination in different ways. Some ideas for accessing different aspects of imagination deliberately include rehearsing something before doing it, brainstorming ideas, engaging all of our senses when imagining something, reframing an idea from a different perspective, and freewriting.

Vieten also suggests creating environments conducive to being more spontaneously creative. Setting time aside to daydream, being in solitude where your mind can wander, taking walks in the woods to de-stress, or, possibly, taking psychedelic drugs (in a safe, controlled environment) can all help us disengage our DMN and allow creative thoughts to enter more freely.

“One of the key ways to make imagination welcome is to remove the practical pressures of the world,” she writes.

Imagine That is full of suggestions for unleashing your imagination, all based on the emerging science of imagination that Vieten and her colleagues (and others) are exploring.

But while the book reads mostly as a self-help guide, there’s also an important message about why using our imagination is beneficial to society as a whole. Too many of us are experiencing the hopelessness and despair that come with being alive right now, writes Vieten. It’s too easy to get lost in the negative news cycles and focus on all of the problems in the world, making it more difficult to imagine anything better for our collective future.

Learning how to engage our imagination more readily can create a sense of hope in our current situation. Not only can it bring more joy and aliveness to our individual lives, countering malaise, it can also lead to new ways of collaborating with others and innovating to solve societal problems, thereby providing a better life for everyone.

“So many of the issues facing us locally and globally are rooted in our collective inability to imagine new solutions, alternative futures, creative pathways forward that could build a world that promotes thriving for all,” writes Vieten. “My deepest hope is that [you] take a deeper dive into the science, the practice, and the magic of imagination and [see] how it can re-enchant your life and our world.”

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

#9602. Give Boxed Cake Mix A British-Style Upgrade With Cream And One Jarred Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Anyone who believes British cuisine falls short has likely never experienced a British cake, with notable example being a traditional Victoria sponge. Much like a classic cup of tea, this dessert represents the essence of British baking, offering elegance through simple ingredients. Even novice bakers can easily prepare one from scratch, but using a boxed cake mix offers a far more convenient alternative. Upgrading a simple store-bought mix into an authentic Victoria sponge requires just one key addition to your pantry: a good jar of strawberry or raspberry jam.

Jam is at the heart of a Victoria sponge. The cake consists of two light, fluffy sponge layers sandwiched together with jam and whipped cream. Early versions of this cake, which trace back to Victorian-era afternoon tea culture heavily championed by Queen Victoria, were most commonly filled with just raspberry jam, no cream. Today, however, many bakers include a layer of whipped cream or vanilla buttercream alongside the jam, although traditionalists still debate the "proper" filling.

Adding jam to a Victoria sponge sounds simple enough, but there is an art to it. Before assembling the cake, make sure that each sponge layer has cooled completely. This typically takes about 20 to 30 minutes after removing the layers from the oven. If you assemble the cake while it is still warm, the jam (and cream) will melt and run, ruining the distinctive layers that give the Victoria sponge its elegant charm. It is also important to use the right amount of jam — too little will be unnoticeable, while too much will ooze out. A helpful tip is to leave a small border around the outer edge of the bottom sponge so that when the top layer is added, the jam spreads outward without spilling over.

The Victoria sponge might be an old-school recipe, but there's always room for improvement. While we'd advocate for experimentation, a Victoria sponge is almost always a golden-yellow sponge. There's no going wrong with a chocolate boxed cake mix, but if you want to keep things traditional (and avoid the wrath of the Brits), it's best to toss a yellow cake mix into your cart. To make life easier, we've already ranked Betty Crocker's Super Moist Yellow Cake Mix as one of the best you can buy.

Although a Victoria sponge might sound simple, there are, pardon the pun, levels to this cake. Assembling the sponge is easy enough, but the jam and cream are where you can really let your baking skills speak for themselves. Instead of jarred jam, you could make your own. Sure, it's not as convenient, but your taste buds will thank you. Simply combine diced raspberries or strawberries with lemon juice and sugar, leave it for an hour, then simmer over medium-low heat until it reaches your desired consistency — or consider making a jarringly beautiful ruby red jam. Let it cool completely before spreading, so it doesn't seep into the sponge. Homemade jam will completely elevate your boxed cake mix, and it certainly won't go unnoticed by guests.

The cream also offers plenty of room for improvement. The standard approach is a thick layer of homemade whipped cream over the bottom layer, but there are some easy (and more flavourful) upgrades. Whip a few spoonfuls of mascarpone into the cream for a richer, tangier filling, or scrape in some vanilla bean paste, lemon zest, or a splash of elderflower cordial for something brighter. For a nod to a classic British cream tea, swap in clotted cream, which will pair perfectly with the jam. To make clotted cream (because you won't find it in most stores), simmer about three cups of heavy cream with an ounce of unsalted butter until it reduces by half. Chill it overnight, and Bob's your uncle.

#9601. For A Juicier Burger, Make It Scottish-Style

Even if you have the perfect blend of meats, some burger patties can stand a little extra moisture to keep them juicy after exposure to high heat. While it may be a less conventional choice, black pudding has a remarkable capacity to make burgers juicier, and the method is actually quite similar to other juicy ground meat recipes.

Black pudding is a type of blood sausage consisting of a congealed blend of oats, spices, animal blood, and sometimes assorted organ meats. The use of oats is quite similar to using milk-soaked breadcrumbs in meatballs to keep them moist. When you introduce a bit of black pudding into burgers, the oats can help retain moisture within the patties, keeping them juicy. This helps maintain a consistent level of moisture without adding excess liquid that could inhibit a good crust.

While you can always use breadcrumbs or other conventional ingredients instead, black pudding is far meatier and more similar to a patty's flavor profile. Rich in umami and seasonings of its own, it adds so much more than just juiciness. Black pudding can also crisp up on a grill, griddle, or in a pan, so you won't be sacrificing texture for the sake of moisture. Using roughly one part black pudding to two parts meat ensures you can taste both and get a proper level of juiciness, even when using lean blends.

Black pudding is something you may rarely encounter in the U.S., and regional varieties can make it difficult to find the perfect one for burger patties. While just about any type can get the job done, texture and flavor profile are important considerations, and you'll have to mix it in properly for the best results.

Black pudding isn't monolithic and ranges from the crisped discs served in a full English breakfast to boudin noir in France. The crumbly texture of Scottish black pudding is ideal and makes it easier to add to a burger blend, whether that's beef or another meat mixture. When ingredients are easy to incorporate, it prevents you from overworking the meat and helps you grill burgers like a pro, achieving a tender result that doesn't firm up into a sausage puck. Scottish varieties also make ample use of oatmeal as a binder, so you're more likely to get that juiciness you want.

Scottish black puddings also tend to keep the seasonings quite simple, creating something delicious but not overly complex. By focusing on a simple blend of salt, pepper, and aromatics, they leave you more room to season your burgers to your liking. While boudin noir is delicious thanks to its blend of spices like nutmeg, these can easily clash with what's in your seasoning cabinet and make pairings difficult. Simple seasonings also let you add more to your blend, so you don't have to worry so much about ratios.

#9600. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9599. Add This Creamy Ingredient To Tuna Salad For A Major Flavor Boost (Hint: It's Not Mayo Or Yogurt)

Whether you like to enjoy it between a couple of slices of bread, spread it on crackers, or eat it on its own with a spoon, tuna salad is an easy dish to prepare that makes use of kitchen staples. Despite its popularity and the many ways you can take tuna salad to the next level, though, many recipes include the same condiment to give it richness: mayonnaise. Sure, there are different brands that each have their own unique characteristics — but what do you do when you want to switch things up without losing out on the creamy mouthfeel? Try using crème fraîche.

This rich product originated in France, and its name literally translates to "fresh cream" in English, though don't let its name fool you. It's actually a fermented dairy product made from cream, which makes it similar to but different from sour cream. For starters, it has a higher fat content, giving it a deliciously luscious consistency that complements the texture of the tuna well. It's also less acidic than sour cream, whose tanginess might not play well with every type of ingredient you want to add to your recipe. Furthermore, crème fraîche typically doesn't have added thickeners or stabilizers, which some consumers may want to avoid. It also has its own unique flavor that's slightly nutty and just a little sweet.

Nevertheless, it can be pricier than sour cream, with an 8-ounce container of the former sometimes costing as much as twice the price of a 16-ounce container of the latter. However, you can transform sour cream into crème fraîche at home with some heavy cream.

The first question you may have about using crème fraîche in tuna salad is how much you should use. If you're using one 5-ounce can of fish, add about a quarter cup of the rich, cultured cream to begin with, give it a stir, and add more if you prefer a creamier salad. Because crème fraîche has a high fat content, you'll want to use tuna packed in water rather than oil to prevent your finished dish from becoming too greasy.

Beyond salt and pepper, there are several additions that will take the finished dish to the next level. Grainy mustard can offset the richness of the crème fraîche, along with some capers and finely chopped shallots. For a kick, you can also add a small amount of prepared horseradish or a few dashes of hot sauce. Chopped fresh parsley will impart freshness, and a squeeze of lemon juice can easily brighten the whole preparation.

Crème fraîche isn't the only thing that will give your tuna salad a creamy mouthfeel and rich flavor, though. If you like a little extra tanginess and want to save money, sour cream may be a perfect base for an Eastern European-inspired tuna salad with dill and chopped pickles. You can also use Mexican-style crema, which is a little milder than sour cream but tangier than crème fraîche and pairs beautifully with chopped jalapeños. If you want something significantly milder, though, mascarpone is an excellent option and lets you get really creative with your seasonings and add-ins, as it won't compete with any of the elements of your recipe.

#9598. Nine Conversation-Starting Movies to Watch With Your Romantic Partner

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Movie date nights have long been a ritual of romance, from first dates to married couples’ standing nights out. You can probably name movies that leave you feeling warm, hopeful, excited, stimulated, and sometimes a little more in love with your partner.

But sometimes, the movies we watch become more than that—they become conversation starters, litmus tests, or unexpected mirrors of our own relationships.

These nine movies expose the underbelly of romantic relationships: the resentments, fantasies, secrets, compromises, and alternative lives that can coexist alongside love. Watching them runs the risk of cracking open a door that would be better kept closed, for the longevity of your relationship.

Last month’s The Invite, starring and directed by Olivia Wilde, tops our list of nine movies you might want to watch without your partner—or at least be very sure you know what conversation you’re signing up for in the post-screening debrief. Each movie asks a question that might be safer left unanswered.

What happens when you say the quiet part out loud?

The Invite turns the dinner-party setup into an examination of everything couples are usually too embarrassed, jealous, or afraid to say to each other.

Angela (Wilde) and Joe (Seth Rogen) portray a married couple whose relationship has become strained by years of resentment and disappointment. When Angela invites their upstairs neighbors, Piña (Penélope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), over for dinner, what begins as an attempt at connection becomes a much more revealing conversation about sex, attraction, love, and what people want from their partners, when they’re being honest.

As Piña and Hawk probe the tension between Angela and Joe—also glimpsed through their apartment windows and in elevator encounters—they force the quiet parts of the other couple’s relationship into the open. The questions Angela and Joe were afraid to ask each other come to the surface, like, “Do we love each other anymore? Can we salvage this relationship? Do you want to be with someone new?”

“Novelty is a powerful aphrodisiac. In long-term relationships especially, cultivating novelty—whether through stories or experiences—is key for sustaining passion,” says Esther Perel, sex therapist and consultant on The Invite, on her blog. “Maintaining a sense of mystery and surprise helps counteract the routine and repetition that can sometimes lead to a decline in desire over time.”

We tend to think of monogamy as a set of universally accepted rules: Don’t sleep with someone else. Don’t cross the line. But long-term relationships are also built on unspoken knowledge about what our partner wants, what they find attractive, what they would never do, and what they might secretly wish they could do. Lifting the lid on that box may reveal that the relationship is beyond repair.

What’s more important: Love or money? Would you risk the former for the latter? Can a couple withstand different answers to this question?

David (Woody Harrelson) and Diana (Demi Moore) are a financially struggling, yet happily married, couple, who are offered $1 million if the wife spends one night with a wealthy stranger, played by Robert Redford. The movie takes a question that sounds like a parlor game and puts it inside a marriage: What, exactly, would you be willing to sacrifice for a life-changing amount of money?

Diana’s decision to revisit the proposal after David’s initial hesitation—an uncomfortable pause that both she and the audience notice—begins her agreed-upon one-night stand.

From there, suspicion and mistrust begin to take hold, gradually eroding the relationship and ultimately pushing Diana toward the wealthy stranger.

What happens when a hypothetical becomes real? When money, desire, jealousy, and pride enter a marriage, it becomes much harder to separate what you thought you would do from what you did.

Indecent Proposal can turn a hypothetical into an uncomfortable inventory of your partner’s values—and your own.

Although it’s not every day a millionaire asks to sleep with a spouse, the question, and the length of the pause before answering, can reveal a lot about both sides.

Can anyone be tempted, and can one handle the consequences of infidelity?

Unfaithful, starring Diane Lane and Richard Gere, is a movie about a married suburban woman who meets a younger man and becomes increasingly drawn to him. There is no grand declaration that her marriage is over, no decision to go looking for an affair. There is simply attraction, followed by curiosity, a series of small choices that gradually lead down a road from which there is no return.

Some people believe that infidelity happens only to certain kinds of couples—unhappy couples, disconnected couples, couples whose marriages were already in trouble. But some people in loving relationships can still notice other people, feel chemistry, or wonder what it would be like to be with someone else.

In fact, that is part of what sucks you into Unfaithful: Richard Gere’s character is a quintessentially good husband—a devoted father, attentive partner, and decent man.

“I often find that the affair is a form of self-discovery. It’s not that the individuals having the affairs want to leave their partners, but the people they have become. They are looking for another version of themselves—which is the most powerful variety of ‘other’ there is,” says Perel in an interview with Goop.

A crush can remain a crush. A fantasy can remain a fantasy. But sometimes people begin feeding the attraction, creating opportunities to see the person again, or keeping secrets that gradually become more important than the relationship they are protecting.

Interesting fact: Both Indecent Proposal and Unfaithful were directed by Adrian Lyne, who’s been married since 1974 to his wife Samantha.

Can you love someone and still need to leave them?

Marriage Story begins with a husband and wife listing the things they love about each other. It’s tender enough to feel like the opening of a great romance, but the film quickly reveals a more complicated reality. Inspired by director Noah Baumbach’s own divorce, the story explores what happens when the things we love about our partner begin to pull us in different directions.

Charlie (Adam Driver) loves that Nicole (Scarlett Johansson) makes people feel comfortable, knows how to handle difficult family situations, plays with their son, knows when to push him and when to leave him alone. Nicole loves Charlie’s determination, his energy, his intelligence, and the way he throws himself into the things he loves.

It is an intimate portrait of a couple who, despite everything that will follow, genuinely know and admire one another.

The film follows Charlie and Nicole through the painful mechanics of divorce: lawyers, custody arrangements, money, competing versions of the marriage, and the realization that ending a relationship does not mean you stop having to deal with the person you are leaving.

Nicole has spent years adapting herself to Charlie’s life and putting parts of her own ambitions aside. Charlie has built a career and a world around his creative work but has failed to recognize how much his wife has sacrificed to support it. Neither is simply the villain. Neither is simply the victim.

That is one of the film’s most uncomfortable truths about long-term relationships: Love does not necessarily disappear before a marriage ends. Their issues aren’t due to flat-out incompatibility; they are problems of identity, compromise, resentment, and the slow accumulation of problems that were never fully addressed.

Another question the movie asks is whether love is enough to make a marriage work.

Gone Girl turns marital secrets into psychological warfare; this is anything but a love story.

Based on Gillian Flynn’s novel, the film follows Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) on the day his wife, Amy (Rosamund Pike) disappears. As the investigation unfolds, the image of their marriage begins to unravel, leaving everyone—including the audience—to wonder whether Nick killed her.

At the heart of the film is a deeply unsettling possibility about how little access we have to another person’s reality.

One of the qualities that relationship researchers have found important is emotional responsiveness: the feeling that your partner understands you, validates your perspective, and cares about your well-being. In other words, a healthy relationship depends less on “I know everything about you” than on “I feel safe being known by you.”

In Eyes Wide Shut, Alice (Nicole Kidman) and Bill Harford (Tom Cruise) appear to have a comfortable marriage—secure in the routines and flow of the life they built together. That is until Alice tells her husband about a sexual fantasy involving another man.

Bill becomes consumed by the idea of what his wife has imagined. The fantasy begins to feel like a secret life, and the distinction between imagining something and wanting it becomes increasingly difficult for him to see.

According to Perel, our “sexual fantasies are a fount of information about our internal lives and the relational dynamics of our partnerships.”

People also can make complicated decisions about whether to disclose fantasies to their partners. Sometimes disclosure can create intimacy. Sometimes people keep fantasies private because they fear judgment or because the fantasy itself has nothing to do with what they want in real life.

Eyes Wide Shut makes that ordinary fact feel like a threat.

Are we living the life we actually wanted?

In Revolutionary Road, Frank (Leonardo DiCaprio) and April Wheeler (Kate Winslet) have built the respectable suburban life they were supposed to want, in this movie set from the late 1940s to mid 1950s. But April begins to wonder whether they have mistaken a socially approved life for the life they truly desire.

What happens when the pendulum swings too heavily toward one person’s idea of the life they could have lived, leaving the other to defend the life they have actually built? In Revolutionary Road, April’s longing for a different future increasingly collides with Frank’s investment in the life they have created together.

Long-term relationships inevitably require compromise. But compromise can feel very different when it is experienced as a choice rather than a sacrifice. A relationship should provide a sense of “we” without erasing the “I.” Researchers have also found that relationships can be important sources of personal growth: Partners can help one another explore new identities, pursue goals, and become more fully themselves.

Revolutionary Road painfully takes us through the psychological unraveling of Frank and April—who seem to experience their marriage as a narrowing of possibilities rather than an expansion of them.

Content warning: The film explores difficult themes involving self-administered abortion, death, and questions autonomy.

Can you love someone and still hurt them?

Closer, directed by Mike Nichols and based on Patrick Marber’s play, strips relationships down to their most uncomfortable elements like attraction, jealousy, dishonesty, and the desire to be wanted.

The film follows four people—Dan (Jude Law), Alice (Natalie Portman), Anna (Julia Roberts), and Larry (Clive Owen)—whose relationships become increasingly entangled. What begins with a chance encounter between Dan and Anna eventually develops into a complicated web of love affairs, betrayals, and shifting loyalties. It leaves viewers asking, “Do we want to be loved, or do we want to be desired?”

The characters repeatedly demand honesty from one another, but when they get it, the truth often hurts more than the lie. They want to know whom their partners have slept with, what they felt, whom they wanted, and whether they were ever truly enough. Yet knowing the truth doesn’t necessarily bring them closer. Sometimes, it gives jealousy something concrete to attach itself to.

Would you still love your partner if you knew the worst thing they ever did?

The Drama takes place in the days surrounding the wedding of Emma Harwood (Zendaya) and Charlie Thompson (Robert Pattison), a young couple whose courtship seemed out of a storybook. Over drinks one night with their best man and maid of honor, they each confess the worst thing they’d done. This revelation sparks disgust and soul-searching, as they’re forced to confront the question: “Do you still love me?”

We all seek unconditional love from our partner. The Drama stretches this promise to the breaking point, complicated by the judgment of friends who also know the ugly truth. If you dare to watch this film with your partner, you’d be wise to think twice before sharing each other’s deep, dark secrets.

Yasmin Garaad is a freelance journalist. Her work has also been published in National Geographic, PEOPLE Magazine, Business Insider, and more.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

When we go straight to analyzing our own grief or someone else's, we are skipping an important step.

Sending reels on social media may seem frivolous or distracting, but it actually functions as a form of relationship maintenance.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

Psychologist and meditation teacher Tara Brach explores how practicing kindness and compassion can strengthen our relationships, ease loneliness, and help us feel more connected to others.

The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.
