#9597. 9 Ranch Dressing Brands With High-Quality Ingredients

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Ranch is one of the most popular salad dressings and dips in the country. But many of the tangy products are made with less-than-ideal ingredients. That's why we've created this list of organic and clean-ingredient ranch brands. Not only do dressings with high-quality ingredients generally taste better due to the lack of fillers, but they're healthier, too. That's thanks to the products being made without artificial ingredients or synthetic preservatives. The fact that you can use less and still get a lot of flavor makes these an economical choice, as well.

Because these brands use minimal stabilizers and preservatives, it's important to know they won't last as long as other shelf-stable ranch dressings. Usually, a bottle of ranch can stay safe for up to three months after opening, but with these companies' products often using real dairy, it's best to treat them more like homemade. That means it's safest to consume these dressings within one month of opening, although some can last up to two months. But with all the different ways you can use ranch, leftovers shouldn't be a problem.

Primal Kitchen was founded in 2015 as a way to bring clean-ingredient condiments to the public. Today, it sells over 80 products, such as organic unsweetened ketchup, steak sauce, and mayonnaise made with avocado oil. The company uses plant-based oils and other high-quality ingredients in its ranch, which has no added sugars or conventional stabilizers. Primal Kitchen Ranch, which can be found in many grocery stores, is also made with cage-free eggs, is certified Keto-safe and gluten-free, and is Whole30 approved.

This product is dairy-free, relying on a mix of organic apple cider vinegar, spices, herbs, and egg yolks to create the rich, tangy taste of ranch. Mushroom extract takes the place of synthetic preservatives to keep the dressing fresh, and the dip's base is made from avocado oil-based mayo. In fact, many of Primal Kitchen's dressings and sauces contain avocado oil because it's a sustainable source of monounsaturated fats that are linked to lowering "bad" LDL cholesterol and reducing blood pressure.

Reviewers have reported the sauce having a distinctly herby taste, with pronounced dill that wasn't overwhelming. The dressing is great as is, but feel free to add a bit of lime to turn the ranch into the base for incredible nachos. Or if you want an unexpectedly delicious flavor, add some edible lavender to the dip. The aromatic flower complements the heavier sauce and makes this a wonderful addition to a chopped veggies board.

Ohio-based slaw and salad dressing company Marzetti was founded way back in 1896. Today, it's respected enough by customers to have ranked No. 32 in the Food and Beverage section on Newsweek's list of the Most Trustworthy Companies in America in 2026. So it's probably not surprising to learn that Marzetti has earned not just one, but two spots on this list.

This first one is for the Classic Ranch Dressing. This product is made without artificial flavors, preservatives, or high fructose corn syrup. It also uses actual buttermilk instead of powder, giving it an authentic tangy taste and a creamy consistency. The brand sells it in a refrigerated 13-ounce option or as a 22-ounce shelf-stable bottle. Fans of the classic ranch have praised the product's taste and versatility, alongside the fact that the larger version comes in a squeeze bottle, allowing them to easily portion out exactly how much they'd like.

Created by a woman who wanted to ensure the dressing she was using was healthy, Tessemae's makes its products without artificial ingredients, and every ranch in its line of six is Whole30-approved and made without any elements harvested from genetically modified organisms (GMOs). The company's Organic Creamy Ranch Dressing & Dip doesn't have any fillers either; plus it's gluten- and dairy-free, as well as certified USDA organic.

The sauce uses cage-free eggs in the base, alongside organic high oleic sunflower oil, lemon juice, and mustard. This results in a thick, luscious mix that's flavored by various spices and herbs, with tanginess from distilled vinegar. The plant-based dressing is suitable for those following a keto or vegetarian lifestyle. And even though this version is different from the original 1950s ranch recipe, it's still great for marinating fried chicken, serving as a dip for pizza, or simply pouring on salad greens.

Walden Farms is so dedicated to customer satisfaction that the company changed the way it makes its dressings. After hearing people ask for cleaner ingredients, it reformulated the recipes it uses for products like the Ranch Dressing. The dip is now made with olive oil and no artificial flavors. It's also gluten-free and low-calorie, so it can appeal to a wider audience.

The ranch is low-carb, too, with only 1 gram per serving. Being plant-based, it's suitable for vegetarian lifestyles, and it's still made with no sugars, so it's friendly for diabetic people, as well. There are 30 calories per serving, and the olive oil base ensures this dressing only has three grams of total fat in each portion. If you're interested in trying Walden Farms ranch, you can use it in your next batch of mac and cheese along with corn kernels for some nice pops of sweetness.

Drew's Organics doesn't use GMO ingredients or any artificial flavors or colors in any of its dressings. That includes the Creamy Ranch Dressing & Quick Marinade, which is made without artificial preservatives, added sugars, high-fructose corn syrup, or trans fats. The ranch dressing also works as a great marinade for a juicy pork roast or chicken, thanks to its combination of fat, sodium, and vinegars. In fact, reviewers have noted the ranch has a wonderfully oniony taste, with a thick enough texture to stick to a salad or side of fries.

It's also made with organic high oleic sunflower oil, which is a heart-healthy alternative to heavier fats, thanks to being high in monounsaturated fatty acids. These MUFAs are associated with lowering insulin resistance, inflammation, and cardiovascular diseases, according to research published in the Annals of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism. If this is your first time encountering it, high-oleic oil acts like extra virgin olive oil when cooking because the two have very similar fat amounts and types.

Toby's Family Foods has been around since 1978. The company specializes in making each of its eight dressings in batches small enough that every one of them can still be made by hand. There are regular sauces, as well as probiotic ones, including a ranch made with yogurt as a base. Toby's regular Ranch Dressing & Dip is made with clean ingredients, such as buttermilk from cows that aren't given rBST, a synthetic growth hormone that's been linked to certain forms of cancer.

The ranch doesn't use artificial flavors, preservatives, MSG, or synthetic stabilizers, so it has a shorter refrigeration window after opening. Instead of one to two months, Toby's recommends the sauce be finished within two weeks. It also uses non-GMO canola oil that's obtained through high-pressure processing to keep as many of the vitamins and flavor intact as possible. That oil can sometimes separate from the dairy in the ranch, but all you have to do to recombine it is shake or stir the bottle's contents a bit.

Briannas has a long line of dressings and sauces made with high-quality ingredients. The brand's Traditional Ranch is a newer product that, while similar to its Classic Buttermilk Ranch, has fewer calories per serving. This option is also gluten-free, vegetarian, and Kosher Certified.

It's made without high-fructose corn syrup, which many companies use as a cheaper alternative to natural sugars. However, large amounts of high-fructose corn syrup have been linked to liver inflammation, making it something you might want to steer clear of in general. Made in Brenham, Texas, Briannas ranch doesn't have trans fats and is manufactured in a facility without the potential for cross-contamination from nuts.

The company has such a dedication to sustainability that each part of the ranch's (or any other dressing's) bottle can be recycled. That includes the label and cap liner. And to be sure the products meet the brand's high-quality standards, the facility is certified by the SQF, or Safe Quality Food, Institute, which evaluates a business according to strict food manufacturing requirements.

Those who follow vegetarian or vegan lifestyles can be assured there's a ranch for them here, too. Follow Your Heart has been focused on creating intentionally wholesome foods since 1970, which is why the company's Vegan Ranch Dressing is Certified Plant-Based and made without GMO ingredients. It's also gluten-free, thanks to ingredients like xanthan gum, which takes over for gluten in helping the product bind and thicken while keeping it stabilized. The ranch is low in sodium, too, so those watching their salt intake can still enjoy the dressing.

The sauce is reported by fans to be a thick, creamy, and highly versatile addition to a snack or meal. One person even claimed that they could eat the dip by itself. An Amazon reviewer said, "This vegan version of Ranch dressing is stupendous and I am re-ordering it. I cannot add enough superlatives to describe just how good it is."

Marzetti's second entry is from its Simply Dressed line, which was launched in March 2026. Coming from a company that's well over a century old, it's not surprising these new products have already gotten good reviews for taste and consistency.

Sauces in this line, like the Homestyle Ranch Dressing & Dip, are made with both canola and extra virgin olive oils. This means it has no trans fats, which is better for customers' long-term heart health. The dressing is also safe for those leading vegetarian lifestyles.

Like the classic ranch, it's made without high fructose corn syrup, preservatives, and artificial colors or flavors. But the Simply Dressed version has fewer calories per serving and is gluten-free. Shoppers can use the sauce as a dip on its own, or it can be combined with a bit of sour cream or a soft cheese to make it thicker and add even more creamy texture.

Determining the ranch dressing brands with the cleanest ingredients was an interesting task to tackle. We first searched for clean-ingredient and organic brands that made ranch dressing before making a list of the dips and sauces that met our high standards. The dressings had to be made without artificial ingredients, minimally processed, and free of synthetic preservatives to make it onto the final list presented here.

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

Get the recipe: Sweet Potato Sheet Cake with Marshmallow Frosting (make it gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” x 13” pan

For a dessert that’s rich but not too sweet, turn to this recipe, which pairs pumpkin and pumpkin spice with chocolate chips. Baked in a decorative Bundt pan, it can be served unfrosted for an easy-yet-elegant dessert.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

Don’t be fooled by its stodgy name or humble appearance: This cake is so good, we named it our #1 best fall recipe! In fact, my colleague Jessica Battilana made it for Thanksgiving last year and declared it the biggest hit of the day; her guests fell in love with the moist, apple-loaded cake and fudgy brown sugar frosting.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

If your biggest complaint about PSLs is that there's not enough coffee flavor, look to this Bundt cake, which has an espresso powder swirl running through the tender pumpkin crumb and a coffee glaze to finish the whole thing off.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Golden Wheat Flour

If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Apples are great, but seasonal pears deserve some love too. This simple cake, made with a combination of almond and all-purpose flours, has a rich, buttery texture and an almost marzipan-like chew. Studded with fragrant cubes of ripe pear, it's an elegant after-dinner dessert.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Almond Flour

The boozy Bundt cake features potent maple flavor thanks to the 1/2 cup (!) of maple syrup in the batter, plus the sticky maple-and-rum glaze to finish. Made with cake flour and sour cream, the cake itself is dense and velvety, like all great pound cakes should be.

Get the recipe: Maple Pound Cake with Maple-Rum Glaze

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

Instead of slicing and serving dessert, bake every guest their own individual mini cake. Start with a moist, spicy sheet cake, then use a biscuit cutter or overturned glass to cut rounds for individual layer cakes sandwiched with cream cheese frosting.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Apple Pie Spice

Rich, silky, and balanced, this cheesecake is the kind of dessert that wins people (even cheesecake skeptics) over at first bite. Pecans are blended into the crust to add a subtle nutty flavor and delicate crunch. The ultra-creamy filling gets its sweetness from brown sugar and maple syrup, while heavy cream gives it an especially luxurious texture.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Maple Syrup

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

For a little French flair at your Thanksgiving table, make this classic tarte tatin. This dessert can be a little fussy, but we’ve endlessly tested our version to make sure it goes off without a hitch in your kitchen. And it’s worth it for the deeply caramelized apples layered over shattering pastry.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” round cake pan

Tiramisu gets a fall-forward spin in this coffeeshop-inspired dessert. Just like a caramel macchiato combines espresso, steamed milk, and a generous caramel drizzle, this twist on classic tiramisu layers salted caramel sauce between espresso-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone filling.

Get the recipe: Caramel Macchiato Tiramisu

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Espresso Powder

Make serving Thanksgiving dessert a breeze by baking up a big batch of cupcakes. These are packed with pumpkin flavor and spice, then finished with an easy swoop of cream cheese frosting. If you really want to level up your presentation, check out these cupcake decorating techniques for a pro-level finish.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cupcakes (make them gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Unbleached Cake Flour

This holiday-ready version of our five-star Everyday Olive Oil Cake is adorned with a big red bow in the form of a simple but stunning cranberry glaze. Made by cooking cranberries with orange juice, then whisking the mixture with confectioners’ sugar, the icing adds a bright tartness that complements the rich cake.

Get the recipe: Cranberry-Orange Olive Oil Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: King Arthur Square Pan

#9595. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

#9594. Not Regular Butter Or Mayo: Use This Spread To Give Breakfast Burritos A Delicious, Crunchy Exterior

Breakfast burritos originated in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and have now become a popular way to start the day across the U.S. — they are even available at McDonald's! The typical combination of eggs, meats, and cheese wrapped in a tortilla is not only packed with flavor and protein but is also a conveniently portable food.

There are many variations on a breakfast burrito recipe, such as changing up the type of cheese or switching up the meats, but these ignore what holds it all together: the tortilla. You can just wrap your fillings in one and call it a day, but you know that it's much better (and crunchier) when you toast it, and you need a little fat to get the job done. Butter is a great solution, but using garlic butter will impart so much additional flavor to your finished breakfast burrito.

Garlic butter isn't some type of fat made from garlic, though. Instead, it's part of a larger category of foods called compound butters, which consist of regular dairy butter blended with a variety of seasonings and other ingredients to add flavor. Since many herbs and spices contain fat-soluble flavor compounds, the butter becomes infused with the aromas of whatever is added to it, including garlic. So, when you toast your breakfast burrito in garlic butter, the fat itself has a garlicky kick that will get transferred to your tortilla. It will also save you the hassle of frying garlic in butter to get a similar effect.

To make your breakfast burrito extra crispy with garlic butter, you simply need to wrap your burrito in a flour tortilla, which is the most flexible for making this breakfast favorite and tends to come in larger sizes compared to corn tortillas. You can assemble several burritos this way if you want to meal prep. Then, melt about a tablespoon of garlic butter in a pan over medium heat and place your burrito in the pan seam-side down to seal it. Turn it over to toast the other side, and promptly remove it from the pan. For more even browning, you can place a flat tortilla in the pan, add all your fillings, and then remove it to roll up, making sure to tuck in the sides. You can also grease a muffin tin with garlic butter to make breakfast burrito bites.

There are many commercially available garlic butters you can find at supermarkets, including one made by Kerrygold, but they can often be more expensive per ounce than regular butter, even from premium brands. Fortunately, compound butters — including variations on plain garlic butter — are very easy to make at home. David Guas' roasted garlic compound butter, for example, can be frozen for up to three months and is customizable. You can add finely minced herbs, like parsley and thyme. If you don't have fresh herbs, you can also use dried versions, though give your compound butter some extra time for the flavors to marry.

#9593. Three Qualities That Can Make You an Inspiring Leader

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Imagine you’re on a plane and suddenly hear an explosion. The whole plane rattles, and you see the left engine is on fire. After another loud noise, you realize there’s a hole in the side of the aircraft. As air rushes out, the plane is rapidly descending—over 20,000 feet in less than five minutes.

If you faced what passengers of Southwest Airlines 1380 experienced, you would probably do what they did: frantically write goodbye messages to your family and loved ones, thinking that these are your last moments on Earth.

But on that flight, the pilot, Captain Tammie Jo Shults, came on the intercom and said 10 simple words: “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.”

The passengers would later talk about how those 10 words were transformative, turning their panic into possibility. By sharing those 10 words, Captain Shults was helping her passengers make sense of their experience and reframe the dramatic descent, from “plummeting to Earth” to a planned and orchestrated path to safety.

As Captain Shults expertly landed the plane, she calmly and peacefully talked to air traffic control. After landing, she got up and went row by row, looking every passenger in the eye to make sure they were OK. People talked afterward about her words, her stature, and her empathy as she walked down that aisle.

Contrast Captain Shults’s experience with another captain who also dealt with a massive hole in his vessel, Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia. Headed out on a seven-day cruise in the Mediterranean, the ship got too close to shore. It’s debatable why that happened: Captain Schettino claims he was saluting mariners on the shore; prosecutors claim he was trying to impress his mistress who was on board. But what isn’t in dispute is what happened next: The rocks tore a 115-foot hole in the side of the ship, which caused it to eventually capsize.

Before calling the Coast Guard, Captain Schettino spent time getting his story straight. The crash had caused an electrical blackout, but he was going to try to say that the blackout caused the crash. He tried to pin the responsibility on the helmsman. It took him almost an hour after the crash to sound the evacuation siren.

While people were frantically trying to find safety, Captain Schettino was nowhere to be found. Finally, the Coast Guard discovered him in a lifeboat—though Captain Schettino claimed that he “accidentally” fell into the lifeboat. But he also somehow fell out of his captain’s uniform. He was sitting in a lifeboat watching his boat sinking, hiding in civilian clothing. You can hear the outrage in the Coast Guard’s voice when he says in an audio recording, “I’m gonna make you pay for this.” And Captain Schettino did pay. He was sentenced to 12 years in prison for manslaughter and abandoning ship.

These two people faced very similar situations. They were both captains, dealing with holes in the side of their vessels, but how they responded to their crises was completely different. Captain Shults helped people make sense of their experience. She was courageous, competent, and calm in landing the plane, and she compassionately connected to each of her passengers. In contrast, Captain Schettino caused the accident, refused to take any responsibility, and did not take any action to help his passengers save their lives. As a result of his selfish negligence, 32 people died, and numerous people were injured.

Why do some leaders create feelings of inspiration that percolate a wellspring of hope and possibility in others, while other leaders create seething cauldrons of infuriation and resentment? I’ve asked this question to tens of thousands of people across the globe, and here is what I learned about what makes a leader inspiring.

My first big idea is that “inspiring” and “infuriating” leaders exist on an enduring continuum that is made up of three universal factors:

We can inspire people in how we communicate, how we present ourselves, and how we interact with others—through our words, our actions, and our interactions.

My second big idea is that these are the three factors of inspiring leadership because each one fulfills a fundamental human need. Being visionary fulfills the fundamental need for meaning and understanding. That’s what Captain Shults provided when she said, “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.” She helped people make sense of their experience.

Being an exemplar fulfills the fundamental need for protection and passion. Captain Shults courageously protected her passengers with her calm and competence.

And being a mentor fulfills the fundamental human need for belonging and status. That’s what Captain Shults offered as she walked down the aisle: She made her passengers feel recognized and seen.

By surveying tens of thousands of people across the globe, I have found these three dimensions to be universal. There is not a single inspiring characteristic that is mentioned in one country that’s not mentioned in the dozens of countries in the world where I have collected data.

Effective visionaries not only offer a clear perspective on the world, but they also make their vision easy to follow and understand, and so engaging that it captures our attention.

The easiest way to make something easy is to make it simple. I call this the Inception Rule, after the movie Inception, where Leonardo DiCaprio tries to plant an idea in someone’s head during a dream. He discovers it’s not about how deep you go; it’s about how simple the idea is. As a leader, you want to constantly be thinking how to reduce your ideas to their simple core.

Another way that we can make things easy to understand is to repeat them, the way a chorus repeats in a song. The more people hear it, the more they will remember it.

Let’s consider Zoom’s vision: Delivering Happiness. It’s simple, and bubbly. But that vision is also deeply practical—it helped Zoom’s employees efficiently make high-stakes decisions during the chaos of the COVID-19 pandemic. As millions of people began using the product for the first time, Zoom needed to decide on its product’s baseline level of functionality. Too many features would overwhelm people, but too few features would stymie people. They needed the Goldilocks baseline of features to deliver happiness.

Similarly, delivering happiness led Zoom to invest heavily in customer service. Most of us know how much an hour-long wait for customer service can destroy happiness. So, Zoom hired many agents so wait times would be as short as possible.

To make our visions more engaging, we can use visual language. Andrew Carton, an associate professor of management at Wharton, did a study where people were told that a company’s mission was to either “make our customers satisfied” or “make our customers smile.” Then, he had people create a product. When they were working under the more visual vision (“smile”), they created more engaging products.

How to become more visionary: We can inspire people to be more visionary by having them reflect on their values. In one of my studies, we worked with a Swiss employment agency. When people came in to register for benefits, half of them were asked to reflect on their values, why those values mattered to them, and how they demonstrated them. For example, my own values include generosity, courage, and kaizen (a Japanese word for continued improvement).

Two months later, the people who had reflected on their values were twice as likely to have a job. The effects were so profound that the employment agency asked us to end our study and give everyone the reflection activity.

To be a great exemplar, the first thing you want to do is to consistently embody your vision; don’t be a hypocrite. As former CEO of PepsiCo Indra Nooyi once noted, “Don’t ask someone to do something that you wouldn’t do [yourself].”

Inspiring exemplars are calm and courageous protectors, like Captain Shults. And they show passion. When you ask someone to talk about a passion of theirs, their eyes light up, they smile a big beaming smile, they speak quickly and dramatically use their hands, and they lean in as if telling you a secret. When we are passionate about something, it’s revealed in our eyes, our mouth, our voice, and our bodies. And when you listen to someone’s passion, you smile, your eyes light up, and you feel the energy inside of you.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series

In my research on Dragon’s Den, which is a variant of Shark Tank, when entrepreneurs expressed more passion—in their eyes, their voice, their hands—they were dramatically more likely to receive funding. You can’t inspire others if you aren’t inspired.

How to become a better exemplar: Think about the moments in your life when you felt the most powerful and in control, your best self. Hundreds of studies around the world have used this technique that my colleagues Deb Gruenfeld, Joe Magee, and I created. We’ve even found that people are more likely to be selected for jobs if they’ve engaged in this reflection.

Consider this proverb by Confucius: “Tell me and I will forget, show me and I may remember, involve me and I will understand.” When you involve people, they feel seen and heard and they feel like people, not objects.

Inspiring leaders empower others everywhere across the globe. Even in cultures that are less individualistic than the United States—like Thailand or Saudi Arabia—there’s nothing more infuriating than when a boss micromanages you, rather than involves you or trusts you.

Inspiring leaders also elevate others. They share credit rather than steal credit, which is one of the most infuriating things that can happen at work. Finally, inspiring leaders empathize with others. They do what Captain Shults did, in making sure each of her passengers were OK, versus only thinking about themselves, like Captain Schettino.

How to become a better mentor: Reflect on the perspectives of others. My colleagues and I did a study with medical students who were tasked with diagnosing what was wrong with patients. Before meeting their patients, half the students were told to take the perspectives of their patients and to think about a recent time when they had engaged in perspective taking. Ultimately, the patients were more satisfied, trusting, and likely to follow the advice of the doctor who had been reminded to engage in perspective taking.

My third big idea is that inspiring leaders aren’t just born; they’re also made. Because there is a universal set of inspiring attributes and behaviors, they can be practiced, nurtured, and developed.

My fourth big idea is that when you’re a leader, you don’t have the option of not having an impact. Your behavior is going to inspire or infuriate. I call this the “leader amplification effect.” Everything you say and do as a leader gets amplified. Your criticisms become humiliating criticisms, but your compliments become glorious praise.

My fifth big idea is that you can REIP what you sow. This phrase, drawn from the Bible, suggests that if we put inspiring energy out in the world, we receive inspiring energy in return. But my REIP is a homonym of reap, and it stands for reflect, emulate, intend, and practice:

My final big idea is that inspiring leaders think like architects. Like an architect who designs buildings to produce particular reactions and interactions, leaders design policies and practices that lead people down the inspiring path, even when they’re not present. So instead of just changing individual behavior, you can think about: How can you change a broader dynamic?

Thinking like an architect moves you from viewing a situation as a person problem—What’s wrong with this employee?—to start to think about what’s wrong in their environment, and how you can redesign that environment to help the employee be the best version of themselves.

Here’s one practice that Joseph Stagliano, president of NBT Bank, designed to inspire those around him. Although he has over 1,200 employees, he sends a birthday greeting to every single person. That sounds impossible, but he does it in 10 to 15 minutes over coffee every day.

The message is simple yet personalized. He showed me an example that said, “Hey Monica [pseudonym], Happy birthday! I hope you had a great weekend? How did track and bowling go?” Although his message was short, Monica’s response was extensive, overflowing with information and enthusiasm.

I shared that idea with the CEO of another company, and then a month later, he told me he started doing something similar. Every morning over coffee, he reached out to one person in his organization, and he expressed either gratitude or praise. He said he did this to put a skip in their step, but they ended up sending him such glowing replies that it put a skip in his step. The CEO reaped the inspiring energy he sowed. You can, too.

This essay is based on a talk that is part of the Positive Links Speaker Series by the University of Michigan’s Center for Positive Organizations. The Center is dedicated to building a better world by pioneering the science of thriving organizations.

Adam Galinsky is a professor at the Columbia Business School. He is author or co-author of more than 200 scientific articles, the bestselling book INSPIRE: The Universal Path for Leading Yourself and Others (HarperCollins, 2025), the bestselling book Friend & Foe (Penguin Random House, 2015), and a popular TED talk, How to Speak Up for Yourself, with over 7.8 million views.

#9592. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

Liz Cahill was born and raised in Philadelphia. Her whole family is from Philadelphia, going back generations. One day, she was offered an internship in the Bay Area and decided to make the leap, despite not knowing anything about it or anyone there.

“I said goodbye to everything I knew and loved in Philadelphia and came to the Bay. Not knowing a soul.”

When she arrived, it hit her. “I was like, wow, I’m in a place that like, literally nobody knows me. So if I am dead in a ditch, like nobody will figure it out for a long time.”

This could have been a story of loneliness and disconnection, but it wasn’t, because someone took her under their wings—actually two strangers, her roommates Lauren and Deirdre. “They took me in and welcomed me and brought me into their whole social world, which showed me so much love.”

This isn’t the experience for most people. Darilys Matos Acevedo grew up in Puerto Rico. “In Puerto Rico, a stranger talks to you all the time. If you went down the street and you talked to somebody, if you made eye contact . . . you had to smile at them or you said good morning or good afternoon.”

Then she moved to Boston for graduate school. “I had never even visited the place. I knew nobody here.” And where she got smiles and small talk in Puerto Rico, in Boston she “got glares.” “And I’m like, oh, OK. You don’t do any of that here.” It was painful and created a large void in her life.

As Darilys talked to other Latinos in Boston, she assumed “I’m the only one who feels this way, but I wasn’t. There was like a whole group of people that felt like that.”

Their stories are different, but they reveal the same truth.

Moving doesn’t simply change where we live. It interrupts the invisible web of relationships that makes everyday life feel familiar, that makes us feel like we belong. And the majority of the 13 million American adults who move each year experience this.

At the US Chamber of Connection, our recent study on social connection in America explored the impact of life transitions on social connection. It found that 40% of people navigating a relocation struggle with social connection, and they report 35% more barriers to connection compared to everyone else. Two of the most common barriers are not knowing where to start and not wanting to go out alone.

The impact is lasting, as someone shared with us. “Two years ago, I was going on a vacation, and I could not find ONE neighbor to water my plants while I was away. I had lived in this building on and off for over 15 years. I was mortified. How could it be that I had nobody in my building to help with such a small task?”

Moving ranks among the most stressful life events a person can experience, on par with divorce and job loss. But the stress isn’t just logistical; it’s psychological. Moving severs the informal ties and daily routines that quietly anchor our sense of who we are and where we belong. The result is a predictable but rarely named experience: not just loneliness, but identity dislocation. The question isn’t only “who do I know here?” but “who am I here?”

This month, we're teaming up with the US Chamber of Connection for Welcome Week. Together, we're mobilizing communities, neighborhoods, and organizations nationwide to do one simple thing this September: open the door to a new friend. Make a pledge to invite someone in and help us reach our goal to make 100,000 people feel welcomed!

To understand the scale of that loss, consider what a typical adult social network requires to build: roughly 200 hours to develop a close friend, 90 hours for a friend, and five hours of repeated interaction for each of the weak ties (neighbors, familiar faces, community contacts) that make daily life feel anchored. A typical adult carries around 1,300 hours of accumulated relationship time. When you move, you leave all of it behind and start from zero.

This is also, paradoxically, what makes the first year after a move one of the most powerful windows for connection. Disruption breaks old habits and makes people unusually open to forming new ones, a phenomenon researchers call the habit discontinuity effect. People who have just moved are more likely to join things, try things, and reach out than they were six months earlier at home.

What closes that window isn’t lack of desire. Research by Nicholas Epley at the University of Chicago finds that people systematically underestimate how much strangers want to connect and overestimate how awkward the attempt will be. Both the newcomer and the potential neighbor hold back, each assuming the other isn’t interested. Both tend to be wrong.

And the effects of getting it right last longer than most people expect. Vanessa Elias, the founder of Block Party USA, shared with us the story of a neighbor who brought her family a pie when she moved in as a six year old. She remembers her name, Mrs. Fisher, decades later.

What would happen if welcoming became a civic practice instead of an individual virtue? This year, the US Chamber of Connection recruited over 250 people across 25 states to run creative experiments that aimed to help others feel more welcome in their neighborhoods. They were trained on the science of connection and worked together across the country to support each other. We call them the Welcome Committee.

For many of the volunteers, they signed up because they had an experience like Liz. One shared that “when we arrived to our new town we felt welcomed, surprised, and alive through these touches, and wanted to build more.” Or as another volunteer explained, “people are still welcoming me and I still feel at home here. So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I wanna create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”

For others, it came from an experience more akin to Darilys’s. “I would have loved to find this kind of thing when I moved,” shared one early volunteer. “I’ve been in my neighborhood and city since 2019 and have yet to make close friends in the neighborhood or city where I live. It feels scary and uncomfortable to get out there. But I’m realizing the huge impact of not having close friends. I’m ready to make the effort. Because if I’m feeling this way, I can’t be the only one.”

They each began by inviting a neighbor for a conversation. They shared their stories of their neighborhoods growing up. Dreamed about the ideal neighborhood together. Explored the Six Points of Connection, a clear and actionable checklist for individuals and leaders to define and strengthen social bonds. And then they explored how they might together make the neighborhood more connected.

They ran some creative experiments. Lindsay turned their suburban garage door into a community message board. Kaitlin created a traveling tin of homemade baked goods that moves neighbor to neighbor down the street, each recipient required to bake something and pass it on to someone new. Sarah hosted a gathering for other people named Sara(h) in her town. Courtney started flyering the neighborhood to organize a dog gathering in someone’s backyard. Nithya left a flower and a handwritten note for each of the five nearest neighbors inviting them to coffee.

Many of the volunteers nostalgically tried things they remembered from their childhood or had seen in a movie. Kate moved an iron chair and table to her front step and started having her morning coffee there facing the street. Jon made lemonade with his kids and set out donuts for anyone walking by. Chet started introducing himself on his daily dog walks. Anne organized a multi-household yard sale across eight houses. And many of them hosted potlucks and block parties.

They all expressed knowing “how meaningful it can be to walk into a new space and find someone who is genuinely glad you are there.” And they wanted to make people feel that way.

As the volunteers conducted their experiments, they began to share their findings. They mirrored much of what we have learned from social scientists over the last 50 years. Four themes emerged that help to inform how we can all do more to help new residents, and any neighbor, feel more welcomed.

1. The first step is the most important. Stop playing “invite chicken.” Many of our volunteers shared a version of the same experience: sitting at home hoping someone would call and invite them to hang out, attend an event, or even just watch Netflix together. They assumed that the people they wanted to call were probably busy or uninterested. Those people were likely sitting at home thinking the same thing. Nobody called. Everyone stayed alone.

Call it invite chicken: a standoff where everyone loses despite everyone wanting the same thing. The barrier isn’t reality; it’s anticipation. Someone just has to go first.

And sometimes, when we do break the game of chicken, we don’t get the response we wanted. When Hazel hosted her first neighborhood coffee gathering, one neighbor texted that he was too nervous to come. She didn’t give up. She texted back encouraging him. He came. At one of Elizabeth’s gatherings in San Diego, a man had been dragged along by his wife, who promised they’d stay just five minutes. He was the last to leave.

We are poor forecasters of our own social experiences. People overweight the discomfort of initiation and underweight the pleasure of connection. The host who sends the follow-up text, the wife who insists on five minutes, isn’t being pushy. They’re correcting for a cognitive error the reluctant person can’t see from the inside.

2. We are more motivated working together. Partner with someone. Erin hosted a neighborhood gathering in New York City and reflected afterward on what she’d do differently. Her top lesson: “I appreciated the help I did get from neighbors and wished I’d had a co-planner to share more of the work with.”

This is consistent with what research finds: People are significantly more likely to initiate and sustain kind and helpful behavior when they’re doing it alongside someone else. A partner doesn’t just make the work easier; they make follow-through more likely, because the social cost of backing out now involves someone else. Several Welcome Committee volunteers named the US Chamber of Connection cohort itself as the thing that got them out the door. Not the training, not the tools, but the fact that others were doing it, too.

3. We gain comfort with repeat exposure. Build a rhythm. Hansen has been hosting a monthly porch gathering (coffee, bagels, same spot) for two years. Recently, he watched neighbors spontaneously make plans to go cycling together and quietly organize to look out for a boy on the street whose father is dying of cancer. Neither of those things was planned. They happened because the same people had been attending his events and they had built comfort with each other. Hansen didn’t suggest they help the boy but had created the environment for it to be possible.

Research finds that repeated contact with the same faces makes us like and trust them more, independent of what’s said. Those repeated encounters build weak ties, which are how people find help in a crisis, how trust spreads beyond close friends, how a community starts to look out for itself. The first gathering gets you in the door. Showing up again is what builds the neighborhood.

What these moments share is spontaneity and clarity of intent. Research finds that unexpected gestures create a positive disruption that formal invitations don’t. They bypass the social calculation people run when a stranger approaches, and they signal warmth without asking for anything back. Research finds that being noticed is the precondition for feeling like you belong.

And having a clear role removes the ambiguity that makes first moves feel risky. When Annie said “I’m a Welcome Committee member,” her motives were transparent before she said another word. You don’t need a plan. You need to look up.

Giving to others produces more sustained well-being than spending on yourself. The helper’s high is real. Welcoming a newcomer isn’t just a form of service; it’s one of the highest-return social investments you can make.

Liz knows this firsthand. The woman who arrived in the Bay Area not knowing a soul, wondering if anyone would notice if she disappeared, is now the person who creates spaces for others to land. “People here took a chance on me,” she says. “So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I want to create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”

All friendships begin the same way: by talking to strangers. Someone just has to go first. Years later, Liz became the person who notices.

Aaron Hurst is a pioneer social entrepreneur and CEO focused on rebuilding human connection to strengthen communities. He founded the U.S. Chamber of Connection to address the national decline in social ties and trust. Previously, he founded the Taproot Foundation, sparking a $15B pro bono service movement, and led Imperative, which developed purpose profiling tools used by over 200 companies. He’s also co-founder of Board.Dev, connecting tech leaders to nonprofit boards. Author of The Purpose Economy, Aaron’s work has shaped the purpose movement in business and been featured in The New York Times, Bloomberg, and SSIR. He lives in Seattle with his family.

#9586. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

#9585. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from upcoming podcast guests Ina Garten (episode dropping November 23!) and King Arthur’s Martin Philip (find his episode November 16), as well as guests from previously aired episodes, including Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her forthcoming podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza dropping November 23, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philips cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9583. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9579. What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” said Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”

Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related issues than average.

Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio said. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”
